title: Animal welfare group calls for accountability after latest racing death
text:
Animal welfare campaigners have called for the racing industry to be made more accountable for racehorse deaths after Ohope Wins was put down following a fall in the Caulfield Cup.

The Chris Waller-trained Ohope Wins was in the finishing straight of the 2,400m Group One race when it was brought down by last year's winner, Half Yours, which had fallen at the 300m mark.

Half Yours got up and ran riderless down the straight, while Ohope Wins was assessed by vets as it lay on the track and was euthanased.

Half Yours received lacerations and abrasions after falling in the Caulfield Cup, but got up and ran to the finish rider-less. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Half Yours's rider Mark Zahra and Ohope Wins's jockey Jye McNeil were taken to hospital for observation.

Racing Victoria confirmed Zahra was released on Saturday night, and McNeil would be released on Sunday, with both jockeys escaping serious injury.

Racing Victoria stewards will hold an inquiry into the incident, although a time has not been set for this to happen.

Ohope Wins euthanased after Caulfield Cup fall A Racing Victoria track veterinarian euthanases New Zealand mare Ohope Wins after a shocking fall in the Caulfield Cup that included 2025 Melbourne Cup winner Half Yours.

The Coalition for the Protection of Horses campaign director Elio Celotto said at least 160 horses have been killed as a result of injuries sustained in racing across Australia this year.

"When a horse falls their legs are very delicately poised when they hit the turf," Mr Celotto said speaking to ABC's News Breakfast.

"They're a half a tonne horse and all they need to do is fall slightly off and it can result in damage to their bones and that is why we see so many horses killed on our race tracks."

He said the racing industry was responsible for deaths on race tracks.

"The racing industry has got a lot to answer for. They say they are open and transparent, they are anything but," he said.

"They really need to be made accountable for the thousands [over the years], not just the horse that was killed yesterday, but all the horses that are killed around Australia simply to make money and for the pleasure of punters. It's simply not acceptable."

Top racing trainer Peter Moody defended the industry, saying that safety improvements had been brought in since a series of deaths in the Melbourne Cup beginning more than a decade ago.

Moody told ABC Radio Brisbane there were less incidents in major races following the changes, including what he called "stringent protocols" horses go through before they are allowed to race by authorities.

Most of the deaths in the Melbourne Cup were standalone incidents, where horses broke down while running rather than colliding with or falling over other horses.

Racing Victoria requires all international horses coming for major races to have one CT scan of the distal (lower) limbs to identify possible bone damage before travel. They then must have a standing CT scan before every start in the Spring Racing Carnival.

There have been no further deaths in the Melbourne Cup since the introduction of scanning requirements.

Mandatory scans for Melbourne Cup runners A diagnostic scan on racehorse Anthony Van Dyck may have picked up on the potential for more serious injuries before his ill-fated run in the Melbourne Cup, a review finds.

Moody described the incident at Caulfield as "very sad and very disappointing".

Moody was asked if there was any way such incidents could be avoided when big fields of horses were running around.

"Whether there were some misjudgements, some horses rolled around in the race, it got tight, one horse (Half Yours) stumbled and dislodged the rider, and then the second horse unfortunately got tangled in that horse and fell also," he said.

"It's just one of those unfortunate accidents. No-one sets out for that to happen. Everyone wants to see the horses and the riders come home safely.

"The love and care and attention [given] to these animals is second to none.

"Unfortunately in all walks of life, whether it's horse racing, a football match, walking across the road to catch a bus and accidents do happen."

title: It's the other spirit of Tasmania but the worldwide whisky business is in trouble
text:
Whisky was legally distilled in Tasmania two years before it was in Scotland, yet the home-grown industry lay dormant for more than 150 years.

Then known as Van Diemen's Land, the distilling of spirits was declared illegal in 1839 by Governor John Franklin, whose wife, Lady Jane, reportedly declared that she would "prefer barley be fed to pigs than it used to turn men into swine".

The ban only eased in 1901 when national distilling laws passed, but it would take nearly 91 years before smaller producers were legally allowed to manufacture the liquor, thanks to the efforts of a man who became Tasmania's whisky godfather.

It ushered in the dawn of the state's booming whisky economy, thriving on the world stage even when it was shocked by jaw-dropping scandals.

Now a global whisky downturn is hitting distillers from Kentucky to Kilkenny and industry giants are bearing the brunt of it, pausing production and laying off staff as customers leave bottles on the shelves.

While the old-fashioned boom-and-bust cycle is familiar for most distillers, the downturn represents the biggest challenge for Tasmania's whisky businesses since the state was governed by colonial law.

Tasmania is home to a third of Australia's whisky distilleries. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

'Let's give it a go': The birth of an industry

Until 1992, small-scale spirit operations were not permitted in Australia, with the country's distillation act requiring people to have built a commercial-sized distillery before applying for a licence.

But that requirement was scrapped after a campaign from Hobart-based land surveyor and pub owner Bill Lark.

Bill Lark and his wife Lynn during the early days of Lark Distilling. (Supplied: Bill Lark)

"The idea to make whisky came … from a realisation that Tasmania must have had good barley because our local beers were being exported all over the world at the time and we knew our water was probably some of the best water in the world," Mr Lark told 7.30.

"And I just made a comment to my father-in-law and my wife, 'why isn't somebody making whisky in Tasmania?' and Lynn said to me, 'I don't know, Bill, but let's give it a go'.

"When I look back, that was the start of the modern-day spirits industry in Australia, opening up the door for ... people to start with a small still and help us to produce good spirits here in Australia."

The Larks sold their first bottles of whisky in 1998. (Supplied: Bill Lark)

With a licence in hand, Bill and his wife Lynn went on to found Lark Distillery, and thanks to some advice from Scottish whisky giant John Grant, released their first batch of Tasmanian whisky in December 1998.

"We had 150 bottles we could take to the market. We weren't sure whether people would like it, let alone buy it, but that sold out almost straight away," Mr Lark said.

" Our second release sold out before it was even bottled and it just sort of grew from there. "

Bill Lark spearheaded a campaign that led to Tasmania's booming whisky industry. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

Highs and lows of a young industry

In 2014, a seismic shift occurred in the whisky world when Hobart-based distillery Sullivans Cove was awarded best single malt whisky at the World Whisky Awards.

Sullivans Cove chief executive Andy Gaunt said the victory "changed everything" for the global whisky industry, and for the distillery, which until then had only been producing small amounts of the spirit.

"It was really a moment that the whisky industry almost literally fell off their chair and realised that whiskies from the non-traditional countries were as good as, if not better in terms of quality, than whiskies from places like Scotland and Ireland and Japan and North America," he said.

Andy Gaunt is the boss of Sullivans Cove distillery based in Hobart. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

Despite its rapid growth and award victories, Australian whisky hasn't been immune from controversy.

The collapse of Tasmanian whisky producer Nant in 2017 left investors thousands of dollars out of pocket, after they had purchased barrels with the promise of them being bought back by the distillery when the whisky matured.

Nant founder Keith Batt last year pleaded not guilty to 736 criminal offences. His case returns to court next February.

In 2022, Lark chief executive Geoff Bainbridge resigned from his role after The Australian published footage of him intoxicated while allegedly smoking amphetamine.

And earlier this year, a Hobart magistrate dismissed charges against the Salamanca Whisky Bar, after allegations it had sold fake versions of the award-winning Sullivans Cove whisky.

Tasmanian whisky is globally renown. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

Challenging conditions

Globally, times are tough. A fall in demand has resulted in Jim Beam pausing production at its main Kentucky distillery for all of 2026.

In Scotland, producer Holyrood has announced an indefinite pause, while administrators have been called into the community-owned GlenWyvis Distillery in the Highlands.

In the Tasmanian town of Port Arthur, cost pressures have forced McHenry Distillery founder William McHenry to let staff members go and scale back production.

"Coming out of COVID, we had two distillers, we had two brewers. We've let both brewers go, we've let one distiller go," he said.

"I largely do all the distilling now, [we've got] a part-time brewer, so the core production side of our business has really contracted a lot.

" 18 months ago we were distilling every day. Now I probably distill a couple times a month. "

William McHenry has had to make tough business decisions due to the global whisky downturn. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

The decision to slow down production is not one whisky producers take lightly. Whisky spends a long time maturing in barrels before it makes its way onto shelves.

That process at McHenry Distillery takes about 10 years, meaning the decisions made about production now won't be felt until well into the future.

"What worries me is that we're out there trying to get overseas business now … when the demand comes, we're going to be struggling to supply," Mr McHenry said.

" We're going to have a look at our bond store and we're not going to have enough whisky there. "

McHenry Distillery is slowing down its production of whisky. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

Mr McHenry said his drop in sales is down to a number of factors, including an increasing number of distilleries, persistently high inflation and people choosing to buy cheaper imported products instead of more expensive Australian whiskies.

He believes the "tightening" business conditions and the increased competition for customers could ultimately lead to some distilleries collapsing.

"It may push a few players out of the market that are either too small or just don't have the stamina to stay in it," he said.

Calls to overhaul excise remission

Some medium-sized distilleries argue the federal government's alcohol excise remissions scheme is stopping them from growing, and contributing to their slowdown.

Whisky producers are charged an alcohol excise at a rate of $110 per litre of pure alcohol, but receive the first $400,000 of excise back as a tax refund.

Mr McHenry is pushing for a complete overhaul of the alcohol excise, arguing it is crushing profit margins for bigger operations who use the money to grow their business or purchase new equipment.

Whisky producers like McHenry pay an alcohol excise of $110 per litre of pure alcohol. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

"Unfortunately, now that rebate, rather than being used for investment in growing the industry, is being used by some distillers to actually cut price," he said.

"It puts a ceiling on the price that you can sell your product for. It strips out all the profitability for people like me.

"It's OK if you want to just operate as a small business and that's all you need, but halfway through the year we start paying [the excise] and we either have to add it to our price or we have to take extreme discounts.

"Neither is ideal, comfortable or pleasant."

In a statement, a spokesperson for Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino said the remission scheme "provides important support to smaller Australian brewers and distillers, helping them manage costs, grow and support local jobs".

Larger distilleries say the alcohol excise is a challenge for their business. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

Keeping spirits high

The challenges that lie ahead aren't front of mind for one of the newest players in Tasmanian whisky, Waubs Harbour.

The distillery, housed in an old oyster hatchery in the east coast town of Bicheno, creates a maritime-inspired whisky.

Waubs Harbour is one of Tasmania's newest whisky distilleries. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

Started by brothers Tim and Rob Polmear, it began making whisky in 2019 and sold its first bottles three years ago.

The distillery has worked to ramp up production as sales increased, and now produces about 12,000 litres each year.

"I'd be lying if I didn't say that I've seen the slowdown in the industry, and you'll definitely see it if you walk into a bottle shop," Tim Polmear said.

"But I think people that love a good premium whisky somehow find the dollars, and fortunately for us, we haven't seen much of a downturn.

"Over the last couple of years, we've seen [a] good 30 per cent sales growth."

Tim Polmear from Waubs Harbour has seen demand for its whisky grow in recent years. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

At a time when others in the industry are downsizing, the brothers are scaling up.

"We're still expanding … we're running out of room in the shed," Mr Polmear said.

Waubs Harbour is a small whisky producer in Bicheno on Tasmania's east coast. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

Production is also increasing at Sullivans Cove. Mr Gaunt hopes that trend continues as the local industry tries to grow its worldwide whisky sales rate from the current 0.05 per cent.

"We have about 3.5 per cent volume share of global wine, and it's taken 20, 30-odd years to go there from when we saw new world wines emerge," he said.

"With Tasmania, a 1 per cent share of whisky globally is what we would like to be aiming for.

"We think with Australia more broadly, that could be up to 2 per cent volume share, which is a considerable increase in whisky that we would be selling and making around the world from today's very small share."

Waubs Harbour produces about 12,000 litres of whisky each year. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

Beyond the gloom

The Sullivans Cove chief executive believes the future is bright even with the current turbulence.

"The opportunity for Australian whisky right now is probably the best it's been for many years," Mr Gaunt said.

Mr Lark is confident the Australian whisky industry, and the business he still represents as a global ambassador, are in good shape.

Bill Lark is not dispirited about the current global downturn affecting the whisky industry. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

"There's no doubt that there are challenging times in the world of whisky," he said.

"We were warned when we first started … there will be highs, there will be lows, and it's simply then a matter of cutting your cloth to suit your measure for those times.

"The interesting thing about the Australian market is amongst that sort of gloom, there's some amazing opportunities.

"It's wonderful to see the Australian market now wanting and accepting Australian spirits. When we travel overseas, the international markets are excited."

Tasmanian whisky producers are confident they can navigate the current worldwide downturn. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

title: Timor-Leste president says first gas agreements to be signed
text:
Timor-Leste President José Ramos-Horta has declared that his country will sign the first agreements for the long-stalled Greater Sunrise gas project early next year, as the South-East Asian country pushes on with the hugely ambitious and contentious development.

But there is still widespread scepticism in the sector about the commercial viability of Timor-Leste's plan to pipe gas from the Greater Sunrise fields to the country's south coast, where the government hopes to develop a multi-billion-dollar liquefied natural gas (LNG) plant and domestic gas facility.

Timor-Leste says that will generate badly needed jobs and economic activity in the country, but the project has been beset with delays, disagreements and doubts.

In November last year the Australian energy giant Woodside Energy, which holds a stake in the venture along with Timor-Leste's state-owned oil and gas company, struck an agreement to "mature and progress" the plan.

Timor's oil and gas gamble The Greater Sunrise gas project was meant to transform Timor-Leste and bring billions in revenue, but locals are still waiting for the jobs and opportunities that were promised.

And Mr Ramos-Horta told the ABC in Sydney that Greater Sunrise was now "finally happening" after "years and years of procrastination [and] deadlock".

"I was told by Prime Minister Xanana [Gusmao] that he's confident that within the next few months they will sign the agreement, [that] we will finalise the three main documents," he said.

Those three documents will help Australia, Timor-Leste and Woodside establish the regulatory and fiscal settings needed for the exploration and development of resources in Greater Sunrise.

Mr Ramos-Horta's government previously said the parties reached technical agreement in Canberra on three documents: the Petroleum Mining Code, Production Sharing Contract and fiscal regime.

But analysts, as well as government and industry sources, all caution that there is still no guarantee that Timor-Leste and Woodside will strike a commercial agreement on a development plan, and that any final investment decision is likely years away.

Woodside and Timor-Leste's government said last year that the first LNG from Greater Sunrise may be produced "as early as 2032-2035, subject to concept selection and investment decisions".

One-third of the Greater Sunrise project is owned by Australia's Woodside. (ABC News: Margaret Burin)

Last month, Timor's petroleum minister pushed the production start date back to 2034-2035, saying the country hoped for a final investment decision by 2029.

Mr Ramos-Horta said the regulatory agreements should be signed early next year after being checked and approved by both governments and Woodside.

He struck a bullish tone, suggesting it was a significant moment for the project.

"We cannot wait much longer. We have to do it now," he said.

"Now is the time, is the opportunity."

An airport built in anticipation of the gas project opened almost a decade ago, but it has hardly been used. (ABC News: Nick Sas)

The issue is urgent for Timor-Leste because it remains heavily reliant on past oil and natural gas revenues invested in its Petroleum Fund.

The lucrative Bayu-Undan gas field, which pumped billions of dollars into the fund over the last two decades, permanently ceased production last year.

And while the fund now contains $26 billion, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) warned last year that it could be depleted by 2038 if Timor-Leste continues to rely on it to finance fiscal deficits without replenishing it.

Mr Ramos-Horta warned back in 2022 that Timor-Leste would run off a "financial cliff" if it could not get Greater Sunrise up and running within a decade.

Timor-Leste has also warned the Australian government that it would turn to Chinese investors to make the project a reality if it cannot secure agreement from Woodside, although analysts have previously questioned whether they would have the appetite.

In the meantime, the airport built in anticipation of the project lies idle, while roads and other infrastructure constructed for the processing hub are beginning to crumble.

But Mr Ramos-Horta said he was confident that Woodside was "determined to follow through" with the project to pipe gas to Timor-Leste.

"It's beneficial to Woodside, beneficial to Australia, beneficial to Timor-Leste," he said.

title: 'Nerves and shame' gone, the DMC Boys look to the global stage
text:
A reggae-rock band from Queensland's Gulf Country are hoping to take their music "worldwide" after opening for one of Australia's biggest acts.

The DMC Boys, hailing from Doomadgee, about 400 kilometres north-west of Mount Isa, recently played their biggest show opening for ARIA-award-winning rock sensation King Stingray.

More accustomed to local festivals and pubs, lead vocalist Elijah Douglas said the opportunity was immense.

"Everyone back home, they're so proud of the band. We've got younger boys who are coming along now and wanting to join in and learn music and sing," he said.

"It's definitely made an impact in our community; now we'd like to make an impact in Australia."

The DMC Boys are hoping to take the music "worldwide" after finishing their biggest gig yet. (ABC NEWS: Abbey Halter)

'Be somebody and something for our people'

At Doomadgee, where unemployment sits around 20 per cent and opportunities can be hard to come by, the DMC Boys have become more than just the local band.

Lead guitarist Tommy Lee Jack said their music gave the community something to rally behind.

DMC Boys lead guitarist Tommy Lee Jack believed music could be used as a healing process. (ABC NEWS: Abbey Halter )

"You just look at all the bad things, and you feel sad," he said.

"We were that kid once upon a time until we realised … music can be a healing process.

"We're hoping that in the next few years we might be worldwide, but we really want to try and be somebody and something for our people."

Mayor Ernie Camp says DMC Boys have shown that arts and music can thrive in remote regions. (ABC News: Abbey Halter)

Burke Shire mayor Ernie Camp said showing the community what's possible was powerful.

"In any community there's knockers [that say, 'You] ain't going to go nowhere' … there are other members in communities that say, 'Anything is possible'," he said.

"But hearing that as a kid probably doesn't mean much until you actually see a result."

A night to remember

The DMC Boys' biggest performance of their career landed on October 10 as King Stingray headlined celebrations for the reopening of Burketown's airport, north-east of Doomadgee, which was flood-damaged in 2023.

Since breaking through with their debut album in 2022, the East Arnhem Land ensemble has toured North America and Europe and become one of Australia's most recognisable bands, combining language and culture with rock music.

Aussie rock ensemble King-Stingray headlined the Burketown concert put on by Durack Civil to mark the reopening of the region's airport. (ABC NEWS: Abbey Halter)

King Stingray guitarist Roy Kellaway complimented the Gulf band's "great songs" and "catchy, hooky melodies", but said success came down to dedication.

"It's just doing what you love, and if you're consistent, and you put hard work and energy into it you can do amazing things," he said.

"The boys [DMC Boys] have done it, it's awesome to watch them, hopefully it all goes well, and they keep rocking."

For the DMC Boys, King Stingray's success offers a glimpse of what's possible.

Largely self-taught, the DMC Boys Outback band boosts culture in February 2026, with more singles planned for this year.

Blocking the noise

But finding their voice hasn't always been easy.

"There were those nerves, shame, like you get a bit of guilt, a bit of shyness," lead guitarist Tommy Lee Jack said.

"So, [when we perform] we put in our minds this picture that we're in the studio… we try to block out all the crowd and just pretend that's where we are."

Despite becoming rock stars across the Gulf, making it out of remote Australia is no easy feat.

King Stingray frontman Dimathaya Burarrwanga said opportunities for emerging artists remained scarce.

"Opportunities are missing; there are so many beautiful and talented artists around Australia that need to be recognised," he said.

"[We need] leadership and having people to look up to … all ships rise with the tide."

The DMC boys are hoping to tour outside the region in the new year. (ABC NEWS: Abbey Halter)

For Tommy Lee and his bandmates, the roar of the stage comes second to their day jobs, for now.

But their message to listeners is simple.

"Never let your dream fall; always continue and stay on your feet," Jack said.

title: War of words erupts as Buti pitches uni merger passion project
text:
First there was Rita's racetrack, then there was Roger's rugby league team.

Now a new name can be added to the list of WA government passion projects — Tony's uni mega-merger.

Senior WA Labor ministers love a legacy piece, and this week Tertiary and International Education Minister Tony Buti went all in on his.

It's a merger of three of the state's public universities — Curtin University, Murdoch University and the University of Western Australia.

It's a move he has been eyeing off for some time, and he says it will ensure WA universities remain "highly competitive, accessible and relevant".

Posters opposing the merger of three WA universities have been placed around the Curtin University campus. (ABC News: Glyn Jones)

But cracks have started to show.

A feasibility study about the merger was reported to be riddled with AI-generated errors, and opposition (including from two of the universities in question) started to mount.

Despite this, a headstrong Mr Buti is pressing ahead.

He even played "an ace" in parliament to drown out some of the noise.

Mixed reactions

Both Mr Buti and WA Premier Roger Cook are confident the merger will create a "once-in-a-generation opportunity".

"At present, we have duplicated offerings, fragmented investment and limited scale across our universities. We have an opportunity to address these challenges," Mr Buti said last Sunday.

Tony Buti says the merger of the three universities is an opportunity. (ABC News: Lauren Smith)

Both say there are multiple pros to the plan, including major economic benefits and improved outcomes for students.

Others disagree.

"Cost, waste, and loss of choice, jobs and legacy will be the hallmarks of the planned merger," a scathing Curtin University vice-chancellor Harlene Hayne said in a statement.

Harlene Hayne disagrees with the merger. (Supplied: Curtin University)

Ms Hayne added it "solves problems we don't have and creates problems we don't need", while Murdoch Vice-Chancellor Andrew Deeks labelled it "nonsense".

UWA chose not to take a formal stance, but its leaders called the merger "an opportunity".

WA's university merger explained The University of Western Australia, Murdoch University and Curtin University could be merged under a WA government proposal. What's behind the plan, how will it work and what comes next?

The political sledging started as soon as plans emerged.

"I think it says a lot that this government might have made its mind up at the start of this process before it bothered talking to anyone," shadow education minister Liam Staltari said.

Outside parliament, the sledging continued.

"News to WA Labor, not everything comes down to a cost-benefit analysis," Greens MLC Sophie McNeill said on Tuesday.

" You can't put a value on the price of our educational institutions like that. "

Opposition's stand

But the criticism that irked Mr Buti the most came from Opposition Leader Basil Zempilas.

On Wednesday, it was revealed a taxpayer-funded cost-benefit report of the merger prepared by accounting firm Deloitte was littered with errors, or "AI slop" as some have put it.

Basil Zempilas has slammed the cost-benefit report of the merger prepared by Deloitte. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"A university student, if they handed this in to their lecturer, they would get an 'F'," Mr Zempilas said outside parliament.

"Yet this is the information that Tony Buti is asking us all to believe."

Inside parliament, Mr Buti unleashed, detailing a private conversation he had with Mr Zempilas months ago.

WA moves ahead with university merger plans Premier Roger Cook says a potential merger could create a "once-in-a-generation" opportunity as all three universities raise concerns about the move.

"It's very interesting the Opposition's position at this stage for the business case," he said.

"[Mr Zempilas] asked me to go outside and have a conversation with him. He said to me, 'My personal view is that I agree with a three-way merger'.

"Not only that, he said, 'I know your side won't agree, but can I stand by you when you make the announcement?'"

A flurry of yelling and name-calling followed as Mr Zempilas angrily denied making the comments.

Regardless, the breadcrumbs were enough for the government.

Rita Saffioti answers questions during Question Time in parliament. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

While answering a Dorothy Dixer question on state finances, Treasurer Rita Saffioti said she was keen to hear more from Mr Buti.

"Well, I could update the house but I'd rather hear the minister for tertiary education talk more about these private conversations," she quipped.

" … It was like you had an ace in the sleeve and you've played it in the parliament today."

Deloitte has called the errors "minor" and said they do not affect the findings of the cost-benefit analysis.

Uncertainty ahead

To squash the commentary, Mr Buti said on Thursday he would ask Deloitte to hand back some of the bill it was paid.

Uni merger 'solves problems we don't have': Curtin Curtin University's vice-chancellor describes a proposed merger of three WA universities as a "solution looking for a problem".

"It's incredibly disappointing. I'm angry with Deloitte. It should not have happened," he said.

Mr Buti might have thought his mega-merger was a lay down misère.

But a slap on the wrist to Deloitte and revelations of a private conversation with Mr Zempilas might not be enough to save his signature sales pitch from further criticism.

Especially if two of the three universities have to be dragged into the arrangement kicking and screaming.

title: Gas company called 'rude' for not sharing decommissioning news earlier
text:
When Hayden Jones and his wife bought an Albany laundromat three and a half years ago, it seemed a sensible investment decision.

The City of Albany, 400km south of Perth, is one of Western Australia's largest regional cities, fuelled by relatively cheap and available liquefied petroleum gas (LPG).

Hayden Jones wants the Albany LPG network retained. (ABC News: Andrew Chounding)

But news earlier this year that Albany will lose its reticulated LPG gas network has put the Jones's business in jeopardy.

"Gas is vital … Without gas, you don't have dryers, you don't have hot water systems, and electric isn't an option," he said.

In January, energy provider ATCO Australia announced it would decommission the Albany network over the next three years, citing aging infrastructure and high maintenance costs.

Redacted emails between ATCO and the state government. (ABC News: Andrew Chounding)

Strict confidence

However, emails obtained by the ABC under Freedom of Information show the Canadian-owned company and the state government had been discussing the network's future eight months before affected customers were informed.

The redacted emails include a confidential briefing note sent to the Department of Energy and Economic Diversification (DEED) on May 28, 2025, under the subject line "In Strictest Confidence: Albany Gas network".

They also show a meeting was held between the utility and Energy Minister Amber Jade Sanderson a week later to discuss the network's future.

Amber Jade Sanderson said the government tried to persuade ATCO to remain in Albany. (ABC News: Armin Azad)

Ms Sanderson said she did not receive a copy of the briefing note, but confirmed she attended the meeting.

"The conversation was courteous, but frank," she said

"ATCO put the view that the network was no longer commercially viable … and that they were considering making that commercial decision to walk away.

"I put the government's view that we would prefer they did not walk away."

Greg Stocks said ATCO should have told the city of its plans sooner. (ABC News: Andrew Chounding)

City left out

News of the 2025 meeting was criticised by City of Albany Mayor Greg Stocks, who said residents had been blindsided by the abrupt announcement, and should have been told earlier to assist the city in retaining the network.

"I think it was particularly rude that ATCO had not informed us and all businesses that they were connecting," he said.

" We would have used that time to try and negotiate with the second supplier. "

In a statement, ATCO said any change to its licence conditions required approval by the WA's Economic Regulation Authority, prompting its meeting with the state government.

"When ATCO began considering the future of Albany gas network, it was therefore appropriate to consult first with the state government," a spokesperson said.

Hayden Jones's business relies heavily on LPG gas. (ABC News: Andrew Chounding)

Thousands sign petition

But business owners, including Jones, say the consultation did not go far enough, and want to see an alternative put on the table.

In August, a petition signed by more than 2,500 people was tabled in parliament calling for the state government to intercede.

"Either a local supplier or the government take the network back, which is what the Albany community really wants," Mr Jones said.

"They want the government to stand up, right the wrongs of the past, and take this network back into government hands."

ATCO customers will have to transition to bottled gas or switch to electricity. (ABC News: Andrew Chounding)

Energy Minister Amber Jade Sanderson said the government was not considering that option.

"I understand that Albany residents are frustrated and angry that ATCO has made the decision to walk away. I absolutely understand, and I share that frustration and anger," she said.

"The reality is this gas network is at the end of its technical life and would need to be entirely rebuilt.

"The least-cost result is to allow customers to transition either to bottled gas or to electrification."

title: Assistant treasurer knew about ATO's credit card ban plans months ago
text:
Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino has conceded the government knew the Australian Taxation Office (ATO) was considering banning credit card payments in July, months before the decision was made public.

The ATO's decision in late September to stop accepting credit card payments from December 1 sparked backlash from the business community.

That outrage eventually forced an intervention from the prime minister and the treasurer to underwrite the costs and allow credit cards to be accepted by the tax office until mid-2027.

Mr Mulino today said he and Treasurer Jim Chalmers were first made aware of the ATO's intentions months ago.

"In July, the government became aware that the ATO was looking at options and that at that point their preference was to not accept credit cards," Mr Mulino told ABC's Insiders.

"The indication we gave to the ATO was that they should continue to engage with the credit card companies, and that there should be a transition period."

The admission comes after the Australian Financial Review yesterday revealed the ATO had privately informed the government about its credit card ban and presented the government with options.

The ATO's decision followed changes from the Reserve Bank of Australia to scrap card surcharges from October 1, which the bank has said was "in the public interest" and was costing consumers about $1.6 billion a year.

Mr Mulino was asked why the government did not push for the ATO to continue accepting credit card payments from small businesses back in July.

"So, accepting credit card payments going on indefinitely, would have very serious fiscal ramifications for the budget, and that's why we always said that there should be a transition period," he said.

Small businesses were informed of the ATO's decision on September 30, a day before it was made public, and given a two-month grace period.

"But the transition period, as it turned out, from stakeholder feedback, wasn't enough. And so that's where the government stepped in," Mr Mulino said.

He was asked if he had any regrets about not stepping in earlier.

"We've changed our position. So I've listened to stakeholder feedback, as has the PM and the treasurer," he said.

"So, obviously we've changed tack and we've listened to feedback. And that's a sign of a government that is putting in place important big reforms."

Earlier this month, Mr Chalmers said he was informed by the ATO ahead of their decision, but did not give a specific timeline.

"The ATO made this decision late in September, not to accept credit card payments. Obviously, we were aware before then that they were grappling with this issue," he said.

Opposition says

Mr Mulino denied the government had a "hands-off approach", saying they "didn't get into all of the details" but insisted that the ATO should continue to negotiate with credit card companies.

Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson slammed the government, saying they "had three months to fix this" and "only stepped in when the backlash got too loud to ignore".

Tim Wilson has criticised the government's approach. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

"At every point the Albanese government has failed to understand the implementation consequences of their higher taxes," he said.

He questioned Mr Mulino's assertion that the ATO made the call as an independent agency, only for the government to then fund the transition period for credit card payments.

"You can't claim it's somebody else's decision while you're the one paying for it," he said.

Government backs down on ATO credit card ban The federal government will temporarily cover credit card surcharges after businesses warn that losing the payment option will put them under pressure.

Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ACCI) chief executive Andrew McKellar said it was concerning these discussions were happening in July when businesses were only informed the day before it became public.

"Business wasn't made aware until just hours before the surcharge ban took effect in October," he said.

"This looks like a completely deficient policymaking process that took small business for granted."

The ATO initially defended its decision, saying it was not tenable for the agency to absorb the $200 million cost and that it would result in less revenue being collected and therefore less funding for government services.

Taxation commissioner Rob Heferen said the ATO "would have preferred to continue accepting credit cards" but that credit card companies did not offer a low enough rate.

Small businesses felt the move was a double standard, since they were expected to wear the costs of the RBA's surcharge changes themselves, and they also feared losing the ability to use credit card payments to the ATO as a tool to manage their cash flow.

Issue hints at leadership tensions

The debacle, and its timeline, has also exposed some tension between the treasurer and prime minister.

Mr Albanese said he intervened after receiving a text from ACCI's Mr McKellar the day before.

Jim Chalmers and Anthony Albanese have faced questions about tension in their partnership. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

"My door is always open. Andrew did text me last Thursday morning, and by Friday morning we had an announcement," he said.

Mr Chalmers denied he was "rolled" and said he and Mr Albanese discussed the issue on the Wednesday prior.

Mr Wilson on Sunday suggested the prime minister "enjoys humiliating his treasurer" and described the relationship as a "psychodrama".

Industry Minister Tim Ayres denied there were underlying frustrations between the pair, and told News24 that Mr Albanese was "a remarkably collegial prime minister".

"This is a cabinet-style government that's working very well, it's very stable," he said.

"It's a real contrast to not just what's happening around the world, but a real contrast to what's happening on the other side of politics, which is a total mess."

Mr Ayres was asked if the government might permanently waive the ATO's credit card decision.

"I don't think that there's any prospect of this issue being managed that way. We've made a big decision to defer this question to allow credit card payments to continue being used," he said.

"There's a significant budget cost to that. It's the right call to make in these circumstances."

Head of ACCI Andrew McKellar texted the prime minister about the credit card changes. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Mr McKellar said ACCI wanted a "permanent outcome".

"We think that will most likely involve a long-term solution for credit card payments to continue to be accepted, but let's not pre-empt those discussions," he said.

He said a key question was how that cost would be funded, and added it would be a welcome step if credit card companies lowered their fees.

"We don't want small business to be left carrying the can for this decision," he said.

title: Sculptors see the fruit of their labour as oranges become art
text:
Sculptures are often crafted from stone and wood but in the southern NSW town of Griffith budding artists are turning to local produce.

Residents are painstakingly crafting art using wire frames, UV elastic bands and fresh fruit for Citrus Sculptures, part of the town's annual spring festival.

More than 100,000 oranges and grapefruits were provided by local growers for the 60 carefully constructed sculptures on display in the Griffith CBD.

About 30 per cent of Australia's citrus is grown in the region, and standards are high.

"We don't want all the ugly fruit on these sculptures," Griffith and District Citrus Growers Association vice-chair Vito Mancini said.

" We want to make sure we have the best on there. "

Griffith's citrus sculpture event was inspired by the lemon festival in France. (ABC Riverina: Jess Scully)

Waxed, stacked and juiced

The fruit is washed and waxed before it is used to ensure maximum shine.

"That wax product actually helps retain the moisture in the fruit, so without it, the fruit would go wrinkly in a matter of days being in the hot sun," Mr Mancini said.

About 600 UV rubber-bands were used to attach the oranges to the orange sculpture. (ABC Riverina: Rachel Holdsworth)

And he should know — he is one of 10 people who worked on the postmodern piece that is an orange made of oranges.

"It's like trying to stack a puzzle together," Mr Mancini said.

" It does take some time, but it becomes a bit of a masterpiece once it's finished. "

At the end of the 14-day event the fruit used in the sculptures will be taken away and made into juice.

Jone Laweloa has been creating sculptures for the festival for almost 30 years. (ABC Riverina: Rachel Holdsworth)

Celebrating multiculturalism

The sculptures also shine a light on the Griffith's multicultural community.

Jone Laweloa has built a Fijian house out of oranges to honour his heritage.

About 10 people helped construct the Fijian house. (ABC Riverina: Rachel Holdsworth)

It took him a week to build the frame and about three hours to attach the oranges.

"This is sort of the house we would build in the villages [in Fiji]," he said.

"So I like to bring that concept back to Griffith."

People from many different backgrounds call Griffith home. (ABC Riverina: Rachel Holdsworth)

Mr Laweloa has lived in the community for 30 years and has participated in the sculpture event for the 26 years.

"We want to show our identity to the rest of the community here," he said.

Griffith City Council tourism manager Mirella Guidolin said there were more than 60 nationalities in the community.

"We have rich cultural traditions because of those many cultures that we have in Griffith," she said.

"[The festival] is a celebration of everything Griffith is about, creativity, agriculture, multiculturalism, hospitality and just the community spirit."

title: A secret diagnosis could have torn us apart, but it brought us together
text:
When Vinko Anthony finally got the courage to tell the love of his life a secret he had been hiding for five years, he had to trust the love and listening he'd given Andrea Zara in the relationship would be gracefully given back to him.

Whether it's romantic, platonic, heartbreaking or surprising, our Love Story series is about love in all its forms. Share yours with us.

These are Vinko and Andrea's words.

There were 20,000 people and there he was

Vinko: In 2010, I was living in Sydney and decided to go on a European holiday.

I was in Dubrovnik; Croatia one morning swimming after doing yoga and I looked up and there was this cuteness overload standing there dancing naked on a rock with no music on and I went, "Oh my God."

It sounds like it was sexual, but it wasn't, it was more Andrea's joy and that someone would have a free spirit to do something like that, he was just having a great time.

Andrea has always and will always have this childlike, curious energy that was the first thing that I fell in love with.

We spoke at the beach but we didn't exchange numbers.

We were both in relationships when we met.

Then there was a big summer festival at Dubrovnik where there were 20,000 people. The reason I went subconsciously was to bump into Andrea again.

I thought it would be unlikely, you couldn't even walk through the city there were so many people.

But the first bar I went into, I was ordering a drink, and I turned my head to the left and there was Andrea looking so handsome in his blue shirt, I remember it so vividly.

Vinko and Andrea communicated via email for three months until they could meet in person again. (Supplied)

2,743 emails between us

Vinko: After Croatia, Andrea and I continued this wonderful communication between us on email.

In three months, there were 2,743 emails between us.

I know the number because I photocopied them all to take to immigration months later when they asked, "Do you have proof of your relationship?"

So, Andrea and I had made a decision that we were going to meet again in person.

He had a wedding in Italy and I said, "Well, I'm coming to Bari, and you come and see me if you like, and we'll go from there."

Andrea had this whole romantic trip planned.

We stayed in medieval castles and villas, and it was a dream 10 days together.

And that was the end of our old lives, there was no going back.

Loading...

Andrea: In January 2011, I came to Australia to visit, and we went to see this woman at the immigration office and she really liked us.

We went there to investigate how we could do the next step in my relocating to Australia and she told us we could officially register our relationship.

So Vinko and I went from the immigration office to the births and marriages office, wearing swimsuits, sweating in 40-degree Sydney heat.

In comes this guy with bleached blonde hair who's never left Australia, and says, "I'm here to marry you." I couldn't understand a word of his accent.

Basically, we got "married" in the middle of the waiting room.

I left my medication where he could see it

Vinko: I had HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) for many years before meeting Andrea and was living a very kind of open life with it.

I spoke to two of my dearest friends about what was the right thing to do in telling Andrea and had written so many [unsent] letters to him.

But I made a call of not sharing it because I wanted to protect us. There was still so much stigma surrounding it.

It was a challenging time, but never during that time was Andrea ever in any threat or danger himself, because I was undetectable and always having checks. But the relationship was under threat because obviously there was dishonesty.

And eventually I knew it was going to come out, but then a day became a week, a week became a month, and a month became a year and then two years and then five years.

But I always believed in the power of love, and eventually I shared it by leaving my medication on the bench in the bathroom, and I knew it was going to be seen.

Vinko Anthony (right) and his partner Andrea Zaza use their own relationship as inspiration in their matchmaking agency. (Supplied: Sealey Brandt)

Andrea: Vinko always had some pills in the bathroom but on this day they'd changed.

So, I was like, "oh, strange" and I checked the box and they were antiviral pills for HIV.

And I went up and confronted him and said, "Is this true?"

But he was right to keep it from me because it would have been the end of us earlier in the relationship.

Then, I did my due diligence into really researching HIV and doing a test myself, and speaking with the doctor to find out exactly what does a diagnosis mean?

HIV in the 80s was always advertised as this scary thing.

This is the problem, you're stuck into that idea and that was how it was for me, until I really understood it.

From a love story to matchmaker

Vinko: Andrea and I had started a professional matchmaking service for gay men early on in our relationship, so there was a lot at stake.

When we sat together and talked about my diagnosis, he was so genuine and so sweet and so kind and said, "We are much bigger than this."

It was like a big weight off my shoulders. I felt safe.

Andrea: We had this feeling we could have done anything together.

It was the support of each other and the achievement of everything else, where it was empowerment, basically.

I never had that in my life [before].

Our love and our relationship are constantly growing. We evolve and develop together, respecting each other and supporting and acknowledging each other’s choices.

It's not always roses, but when you get older, you understand that the relationship gets better and better with time.

title: Women's group vows they're 'not going to get grey hair and do it quietly'
text:
To join any of the 370 Aussie Red Hatter chapters across Australia you must be a woman over 50 with a flair for dressing up, have an instinct for fun, and a royal name.

Anne Darling, aka Lady Darling Buds of May, is a founding member of South Wollongong's Ruby Ragers, an offshoot of the internationally renowned Red Hat Society.

The society started in the US in 1998 and quickly spread to more than 30 countries, as thousands of women across the globe celebrated a social club prioritising fun and friendship.

"We are a worldwide group of ladies, and it's purely a social group that connects, supports and encourages women in their pursuit of fun, friendship, freedom, fulfilment and fitness," Ms Darling said.

"When you're younger you compete with each other but that doesn't happen in this group.

"We're happy to share, discover and explore new interests constantly."

Aussie Red Hatters

The Queensland Girlfriends Giggle 2026 is the 16th convention for Aussie Red Hatters and the sixth one coordinated by Michelle Johnsson, aka Queen Desiderata from Brisbane Western Suburbs.

Women from the Aussie Red Hatters society performed the Hokey Pokey back in 2015, now they plan to do it again. (Supplied: Michelle Johnsson)

With 328 ladies registered from across Australia, the theme for October's event is fun and flowers, said Ms Johnsson, whose chapter is the wonderfully alliterative Magnificent Mesmerising M'Ladies.

Conventions organised by Ms Johnsson have taken place across the state, with this year's meet spotlighting Brisbane's Goodna Jacaranda Festival.

"On Friday we've got boats cruising to see the jacaranda trees in bloom, then on Saturday we're going to the Goodna Jacaranda Festival to do a flash mob dance to the hokey pokey," Ms Johnsson said.

" Little old ladies with grey hair, they get overlooked quite a bit, and that's the theme of the Red Hatters — that we're not going to get grey hair and do it quietly. "

Magnificent Mesmerising M’ladies and their Queen Desiderata at the Queensland Girlfriends Giggle, at Brisbane's Hilton Hotel in 2011. (Supplied: Michelle Johnsson)

The 75-year-old convenor said the goal was, as always, to "have a lot of fun".

"We've got an op-shop subgroup, a reading group, a coffee group and we've got really strong card players, and of course we've got a dance troupe who have been dancing for 18 years together now and we just have fun," she said.

"Two-thirds of my ladies are single, so it's their social life."

Women just want to have fun

The Ruby Ragers, a group of 50 ladies, held their first meeting in 2012 and a website, Aussie Hatting, lists nationwide chapters, events and notices.

"The Red Hat Society started in America in 1998 and the Australian group have the same name, but we aren't affiliated with them," Ms Darling said.

" We've just taken the idea and run with it, and it's been going in Australia probably 25 years. "

As this memento of the group depicts, members of the Aussie Red Hatters are a playful lot. (ABC Illawarra: Sarah Moss)

A poem written in 1961 by English poet Jenny Joseph, titled Warning, inspired the society.

"It was after the war years and she was tired of having to scrimp and save and she said when she got older she's going to do things she could never do, and would never have been allowed to do, like wear clothes that didn't match, hence the red hat and the purple clothes," Ms Darling said.

"An America woman saw the poem in England, thought it would be a good joke to send to her friend and bought her a red hat and a purple outfit."

And that is where it started, a simple poem reflecting on the theme of aging.

Loading...

The Ruby Ragers

Whilst being a member of the society requires one to have a royal name, having an alter ego also helps says Deborah Ricketts, Queen of South Wollongong's Ruby Ragers.

"I think wearing this outfit gives you the confidence to go beyond what you would normally do yourself," she said.

Deborah Ricketts, Wollongong's Ruby Ragers Queen Lunch-alot with her vice Red Hatter, Lady Laugh-a-lot. (ABC Illawarra; Sarah Moss)

"In my normal dress I wear plain jeans and T-shirts but come to Red Hats and I've got bling galore.

"It's purely a social group, we don't raise money or anything special other than have fun."

For the past 12 years, Irma Facey, Duchess of Bling Bling, has rummaged through opportunity shops for purple clothes and red hats to wear at the monthly outings.

"On my own I feel quite silly but with the whole group we just love it and we get so many comments, so many questions, people come up and say, 'Oh, you all look beautiful,'" she said.

"So, we're out there alright, it's just little girls dress-ups, but we're not little girls anymore," she said.

Aussie Red Hatter Marion Keating enjoys her monthly get-togethers with other members. (ABC Illawarra: Sarah Moss)

title: 'Outstanding' Tonga puts England on the brink of World Cup elimination
text:
Coach Kristian Woolf says Tonga showed off its new-found "depth and quality" in marching past England at the Rugby League World Cup.

The result left the English at risk of missing the semifinals for the first time.

With His Majesty King Tupou VI and Crown Prince Tupouto'a 'Ulukalala among the sellout 18,302 crowd in Perth on Saturday night, Tonga controlled the game when it counted, for a 30-12 win.

"We got more and more confident. What I liked the most was the way we defended; we put ourselves under pressure a couple of times, but our defence was outstanding," Woolf said after the game.

"You could see how much the game meant to us, and we showed that in our effort, and it's something that will carry us through the tournament."

The Mate Ma'a got better as the game went on, powering away from the world number three side to seal a victory which puts them in the box seat to reach the semifinals.

Kangaroos halfback's World Cup over Mitchell Moses will play no further part in Australia's Rugby League World Cup campaign after suffering a calf injury.

A first-half try to Stefano Utoikamanu set up a 10-0 lead at the break. But an early score from AJ Brimson was quickly countered, with two tries to Haumole Olakau'atu and one from Tolutau Koula asTonga ran away with the game.

A try to Dominic Young with under 20 minutes to go was only a consolation for England.

"We've done some special things with the Tonga team, but we're still quite new to beating tier-one nations, and England are that – they're a very strong team. We knew they would come out and be physical, and challenge us in different ways," Woolf said.

"It's a continuation of a journey that we're on. If you look at some of the young guys and some of the guys who are a little bit more experienced now, the experience they've got over the last three or four years has been outstanding.

"It's put us in a really good position. They're getting better and better. We've got depth and quality, and we can go and do something with it now."

Team Tonga took their bows to the big crowd in Perth after wrapping up a vital win over England. (Getty Images: Janelle St Pierre)

The defeat is a huge blow to England's chances.

England (or previously Great Britain) has never failed to reach the final four at a Rugby League World Cup.

This result leaves Brian McDermott's team likely to fall short, given the format of the competition.

The team was playing for the first time since losing to Australia in Leeds in November last year.

"It was a really good contest, and when it wasn't a contest, that was probably more to do with us in the errors that we made," McDermott said.

"They're a big team, strong team, and they've got some tremendous players in there. And I thought we we stuck toe-to-toe with them for nearly all the game."

England has to beat France on October 24 and Papua New Guinea on October 30 and hope other results and scores go their way, as they try to finish in the top two of the combined six-team Pool B and C.

Should England and Samoa end up with the same number of wins, the tiebreaker will be which nation has the better points-for-and-against differential.

With Samoa opening its campaign with a 78-4 smashing of France, it leaves England needing to post massive wins in its remaining two games to stay alive.

ABC/AAP

title: Basque migrants transformed town and left behind heritage handball court
text:
Most tourists don't even realise they visit Trebonne as they pass through the town en route to a famous north Queensland waterfall.

They drive through without stopping at the heritage-listed handball court that holds stories of workers who saved an industry and a culture that is experiencing a resurgence.

But Basque woman Marie-V Wherry has always delighted in telling people she is from the town just outside Ingham.

Marie-V Wherry grew up in Trebonne when the town was thriving with Basque migrants. (ABC News: James Tugwell)

"Trebonne was the centre of Basque civilisation in Australia, and I was always very proud to say that," she said.

"Then you'd have to explain who the Basques were."

The Basques are a European ethnic group from an area across France and Spain who have preserved their own language and culture.

Migrant 'saviours'

Three migrant recruitment drives, known as operations Emu, Eucalyptus and Kangaroo, brought at least 700 Basque workers to north Queensland in the 1950s to manually harvest sugar cane.

The Basque flag painted on the handball court in Trebonne. (ABC News: James Tugwell)

Historian and adjunct James Cook University lecturer Bianka Vidonja Balanzategui said the Basques, along with the Italians, were "saviours of the sugar industry" during the post-WWII labour shortages.

And they brought their culture with them.

A Basque man competing in a traditional weightlifting challenge, known as harrijasotze, in Ingham. (Supplied: Gloria Totoricaguena Egurrola, Australia Vasconia and the Lucky Country)

In 1959, a fronton or Basque handball court was built beside Trebonne pub to play pelota mano, a traditional game where competitors hit a ball against a wall and try to score points against their opponent.

Today, it's one of only two left in the country.

"This game is of particularly strong cultural importance," Dr Vidonja Balanzategui said.

"These men were young, active and fit and they brought with them their culture — their distinctive foods, their games. It was very important to them."

Centre of the community

Ms Wherry's parents were migrants and owned the bakery next to the pub and their house, where she still lives, was where people came knocking looking for a goat-skin ball to play with.

She remembers going to the town's butcher every day to get meat fat, which had been set aside for her, to rub on the ball to make it harder and fly faster.

Felix and José Maria Jayo (left) won the first ever game at the court against Juan Cruz Arriaga and Tomas Monasterio (right) in 1959. (Supplied: Bianka Vidonja Balanzategui)

And then, for a couple of shillings if she was lucky, she would watch the men play and score with chalk on the side of the concrete court.

In the evenings, her father would ice his hand, swollen from playing pelota mano, while his wife lectured him that he was too old to keep playing.

"Trebonne was humming in those days," Ms Wherry said.

The town had two grocers, a service station, two bakers, a sawmill, a post office, a pub, a butcher and its own petrol pump. But everything revolved around the handball court.

The two local schools held fairs on the court. It was a roller-skating rink and a skate park, and hosted dances and barbecues for the entire community.

Marie-V Wherry demonstrating how pelota mano was played on the fronton or handball court in Trebonne. (ABC News: James Tugwell)

"That was the gathering point: people coming to play pelota," Ms Wherry said.

The Basque canecutters from 200 kilometres south in Ayr would travel to Trebonne to play on the court and share news from their homeland.

Mechanisation and the end of an era

Dr Vidonja Balanzategui said Trebonne was a "home away from home" for the migrant workers.

Bianka Vidonja Balanzategui says Basque migrants always bring their culture with them. (ABC News: James Tugwell)

But the introduction of the mechanical harvester in the 1970s reduced the need for physical labourers and ended the Basque golden era in north Queensland. Most returned home.

The sound of the ball being hit against the wall has stopped. Local kids never learnt the rules for pelota mano.

The court cracked and became uneven and was eventually earmarked for demolition.

But it was saved by Hinchinbrook Shire Council, which acquired the site.

And in 2001 it was listed on the Queensland Heritage Register for its importance to the state's history and cultural heritage.

A mural of remembrance

In 2011, a mural was painted on the court depicting men playing pelota mano.

A mural was painted on the court in 2011 to make it look as if people were still playing pelota mano. (ABC News: James Tugwell)

"By putting the mural on it … our hope was that rather than tourists passing by on the way to Wallaman Falls, that they would actually stop, look and think for a moment: 'Oh look, there's people playing — oh no it's a mural' and might understand a little bit of the history of migration to our community and how important it was to both the economy and the cultural life of our district," Dr Vidonja Balanzategui said.

She said Trebonne was now "a shadow of its former self".

In May, Trebonne's pub called final drinks. The 430 locals were devastated.

They are left with only a nursing home, a state school and a mechanic.

A sign at the entry into Trebonne from Ingham in north Queensland. (ABC News: James Tugwell)

Yet Dr Vidonja Balanzategui said there was a renewed interest across Australia in Basque culture, food and language, especially in Sydney, which has the country's only other pelota mano court.

"Even though Trebonne might not offer all those facilities that it once had … Basque culture is not irrelevant today, even though the handball court, for instance, is no longer used," she said.

"The Basque community is vital … because it has young people that are interested."

A love for all things Basque

Occasionally in a cafe or shop, Ms Wherry will hear someone speaking Basque.

She cannot help but introduce herself and tell them about the Basque history in north Queensland and the handball court, her handball court, that was the centre of the Basque community.

"It's important that we do share that history and there is something that reminds us that Basque people were in Trebonne and Trebonne was important once," Ms Wherry said.

"We still are."

The Sydney Marathon has introduced guaranteed entry for local runners for the 2027 race under one condition; they have to have completed at least 10 prior Sydney Marathons. While once a measly 3000 or 4000 people ran in the event, popularity has surged, particularly in the past two years after the marathon was granted world major status. Now more than 123,000 people enter the general ballot for 40,000 places, with Australians vying for a spot on the startline against runners from 139 other countries. Viv Kartsounis is a member of the Sydney Marathon Bridge Club. Wolter Peeters The Sydney Marathon has long recognised the group of just under 100 runners who are members of the Bridge Club. That club consists of athletes who have run at least 10 previous Sydney Marathons as members. Before this year, the benefits of being in that club involved little more than some free merchandise and having their names enshrined on the event website. There was no need for a guaranteed entry before the race was afforded major status because there was no risk of missing out on a place at the North Sydney starting line.

Advertisement

But the surge in popularity has meant even Bridge Club members started missing out. In response to their dismay last year, race organisers said they were revising their ballot for 2027 and now, 100 spots have been set aside for Bridge Club members ahead of the general ballot closing on Monday. Because the club’s membership is currently less than 100, all will be guaranteed a spot for the 2027 race, which will be run on Sunday, August 29. It’s a privilege that had previously only been extended to an even more exclusive club of six runners, known as the Blue Line Legends, who have run every race since 2001. Competitors in the 2026 Sydney Marathon. Getty The guaranteed entry has been years in the making for the race’s most loyal runners. “You would be side by side with your friend at the start until the world major started,” Viv Kartsounis, 62, said. Kartsounis has run 16 Sydney Marathons. “But now you have to understand it’s a world major. It’s a huge event.”

Though Kartsounis has been able to bag a spot in the two years in which the race’s popularity has surged, not everyone has been as lucky. Soonchil Shin, 59, has finished 15 Sydney Marathons but missed out on a place in the 2026 race. Viv Kartsounis has finished 16 previous Sydney Marathons. Wolter Peeters “When I first heard about Sydney Marathon becoming a candidate, I was excited actually because a lot of people [would] come to Australia, and it’s good for business, good for the economy,” Shin said. “This year, I missed out even though I uploaded my application for the ballot. But, I wasn’t chosen, I wasn’t taken. It was surprising.”

Advertisement

Blogger Brian Rock analysed the data from those who finished the 2026 race and found that Australians made up 90 per cent of the field in 2023 but just 39 per cent of the total runners this year. Disappointed, Shin was one of several Bridge Club runners who contacted race organisers about missing out. Kartsounis’ collection of medals from racing in the Sydney Marathon. Wolter Peeters “I sent a private message saying ‘you didn’t look after Bridge Club members’,” he said, adding that he mentioned the New York Marathon in his message, which, along with several schemes to lock in places for local runners, has guaranteed entry for those who have done 15 or more previous editions. Organisers told Shin they were looking into it. Then, last month, club members received an email in the days before the general ballot opened to tell them 100 spots had been set aside for its members, meaning all would get a spot in the 2027 race.

Advertisement

The initiative was introduced alongside a separate ballot for those who have volunteered at the race in previous years. Related Article Sydney Marathon ‘It doesn’t sit right’: Sydney Marathon to change ballot after local runners miss out “We remain grateful to the runners who have shaped this event over so many years, and we look forward to celebrating many more finish lines together,” a spokesperson said. “I was so happy,” Shin said. “And it sounded right because we always love [the] Sydney Marathon and suddenly, we [were] just forgotten. I was surprised they didn’t recognise us as loyal customers, and they just forgot about it. And then finally they looked after us, so I’m happy.” Kartsounis felt similarly.

Advertisement

“After all the loyalty, and not only me, other people … There was still no guarantee that they would get in. So all the people that have been loyal all these years, I think it’s great the Sydney Marathon are recognising them – and it will encourage more people, I think, to do 10,” she said. title: Before weighing into the immigration debate, spend a night in hospital
text:
Advertisement

NationalImmigration Opinion Before weighing into the immigration debate, spend a night in hospital Brendan Nicholson Writer October 18, 2026 — 1:30pm

October 18, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

It’s time for a serious reality check. Anyone trying to weigh the so-called “immigration debate” should spend some time in an Australian hospital. Anyone who has spent time in an Australian hospital knows that the healthcare system runs on the labour of migrants. Getty Immigration is being used cynically as a political wedge by those harking after a long-gone monoculture without regard for facts or practical consequences. I recently spent several days in hospital where my experience before, during and after an operation demonstrated how deluded and dangerous this low-grade politics is. Any healthcare experience is a reminder that more than half the Australian population was born overseas or has at least one parent born overseas. My blood samples were taken days before by technicians of Nepalese and Indian heritage. The taxi driver who turned up at 5.40am to take me to hospital was a cheerful bloke from Delhi who took me straight to the correct entrance in a sprawl of medical facilities.

Advertisement

Related Article Opinion

Immigration I’m sick of immigration being blamed for problems it doesn’t cause Ross Gittins Economics Editor I was prepared for my operation by a nurse of Nepalese origin. Then I was put under by an alert anaesthetist from India who’d rung me in advance to check on a mistake I’d made in my paperwork. The surgery was carried out by an excellent doctor of Pakistani origin, who explained carefully and clearly before the operation what would be done, and why. Over the next five days I was cared for by nurses whose families were from India, Nepal, the Philippines, Tibet and Ethiopia; a cosmopolitan mix of Muslims, Hindus, Christians and others, along with several we would once have classified as Anglo-Celtics. If the politicians pushing the anti-immigration line could instantly send most of these people “home”, those of us connected to medical devices would have awakened to a largely still and silent building, sadly missing their skills and cheerful approach. The anti-immigration lot will throw up their hands and say that of course they don’t mean to banish “those” immigrants. That’s not the point.

Advertisement

The reality is that with an ageing population and declining birthrate, cynically harking back to the White Australia era risks unleashing racism that can dishearten and discourage people that our workforce badly needs. Loading That lowest common denominator debate and the way it’s being delivered – basically blaming immigrants for everything – is highly offensive, unsophisticated and riddled with misinformation and contradictions. Having a multicultural society brings great benefits and we’ll be in serious trouble if they all go “home”. Certainly, fix any rorts but leave the rest alone. Related Article Opinion

Immigration Why no number of new migrants will ever satisfy Australian-born citizens Parnell Palme McGuinness Columnist and communications adviser

Advertisement

Otherwise, who will fill the huge gaps among highly skilled specialists across many professions, not only in medicine. Who will care for our elderly and those in the NDIS, staff our supermarkets, pick our fruit, build our houses – not to forget providing flair, skill and glamour in our assorted football codes? Just over half the doctors newly registered in Australia in recent years obtained their primary medical qualifications overseas. Well over a third of medical specialists in Australia are internationally trained. At least a third – and probably more – of nurses in Australia were born overseas and about 17 per cent of them obtained their nursing qualifications before coming to Australia. The rest studied nursing in Australia. Well over 40 per cent of Australia’s aged and disability carers and registered nurses were born overseas.

Advertisement

Those in the medical profession who were born abroad are aware of the anti-immigration rhetoric and say it’s not unique to Australia. A willingness to blame migrants for personal or financial difficulties drives such movements in countries including the US, Germany, The Netherlands and Britain. They note that migrants who establish businesses are often very ambitious and entrepreneurial. Many have done so to pursue new ideas, to utilise their skills and experience, to achieve greater financial and professional independence. Others because it took time to have their overseas qualifications recognised, to overcome language barriers, or because they had limited local networks. Some made a strategic decision to establish a business to utilise their cultural knowledge, international experience, professional skills and connections with overseas markets. Over time, these professionals say, self-employment rates among migrants have reached or exceeded those of the broader Australian population and about a third of small businesses in Australia are owned by migrants. Other assumptions made about immigrants are simply wrong, as in the idea that those accepted in Australia as refugees will be a lifelong drain on the rest of us. Related Article Opinion

Immigration nation I am the child of an immigrant. So are 51 per cent of Australians Eryk Bagshaw Investigative reporter

Advertisement

It shouldn’t surprise that some of those brave and enterprising enough to escape horrors in their homelands, also demonstrate significant entrepreneurial skills once they settle in Australia. We benefit enormously from this injection of talent and drive. On the day before my hospital visit, my hair was cut by a man who was born in Iraq and later escaped to Turkey as a refugee. He made it to Australia, runs his own business and speaks Arabic, Turkish and English. A highly skilled immigrant who has prospered in Australia, he observed that there were, of course, some flaws in Australia’s migration system, and the government was working to address them. But, he said, most migrants worked extremely hard and were not dependent on Centrelink payments. “Migrant-owned businesses make an important contribution to Australia’s economy through employment, innovation, investment and economic activity, while also providing migrants with an alternative pathway to professional and financial independence,” he said. Those driving the toxic and superficial immigration debate need to consider the practical realities of our country and the talented and diverse mix of people who make it work.

Advertisement

A big part of this is noticing what our migrant population does for all of us and thinking through what our nation would be like without them. Poorer in every way. Brendan Nicholson is a Sydney writer. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up for our Opinion newsletter.
