title: Northern rivals aren’t the All Blacks: Why bruised Wallabies still have spring tour belief
text:
Advertisement

SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby Northern rivals aren’t the All Blacks: Why bruised Wallabies still have spring tour belief Iain Payten October 18, 2026 — 1:27pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Star flanker Fraser McReight says the Wallabies will embark on the spring tour bruised but still armed with belief, having taken harsh lessons from a one-sided Bledisloe Cup campaign and knowing they won’t face any sides in the UK with the same attacking potency as the All Blacks. Having gone six games undefeated – the latter five under new coach Les Kiss – the Wallabies came down to earth with a giant thud during a brutal eight-day stretch against New Zealand, in which the Kiwis thumped Australia by a combined score of 93-40 in two dominant victories. Loading The All Blacks effectively repelled the Wallabies’ attack, and were a class above with the ball, scoring 14 tries to six during the series with breakdown dominance and skill. Dave Rennie’s side scored six tries in a white-hot opening half at Accor Stadium on Saturday, ending the contest well before half-time. The humbling trans-Tasman series was a massive reality check for the Wallabies ahead of a big spring tour in November, in which they will play England, Scotland, Wales and a yet-to-be determined fourth side in the Nations Championship finals.

Advertisement

But Australian players were attempting to keep a sense of perspective after Saturday’s game, based on the quality of the All Blacks’ performance, to ensure all confidence gained this winter isn’t stripped away. Fraser McReight (white headgear) makes a tackle on Peter Lakai in Sydney on Saturday. AP “If we were saying we’re going to go into the Bledisloe unbeaten, we’re taking that,” McReight said. “We beat some really good teams, had some tough opposition and some tough, close games. But the ABs are world class for a reason. They’re top two in the world and I don’t think there’s many teams that attack like that: very fast and direct and decisive. “It was a great test for us, and we learned a lot last week, albeit the scoreline wasn’t great. Same for today, we’ll learn a lot. You just can’t give a team 22 points – given they’re the top two in the world – can’t give them 22 points head start.” McReight repeated the point about the potency of the world No.2 All Blacks when asked about the Wallabies’ belief heading into the spring tour.

Advertisement

“No other teams in the northern hemisphere that we’re versing – I guess Scotland maybe a little bit, but not at the ABs’ level – attack like that,” he said. Max Jorgensen tries to conjure something for the Wallabies. Getty Images “So for us, we’re versing the best and adapting to the best, so what’s next rung? England’s first up, they love a high high-kick game, they’ve got some big forwards, quick outside backs. “It is tough over there, but we really relish northern hemisphere teams and especially playing in England. In ’24 we had a great win and last year we’re in that match until the kind of 65th minute, and it kind of went away from us. So the belief is there, and we’ve just got to keep working and taking lessons.” “Lessons” are a modern-day go-to for a losing dressing room, but the return of several significant starting players for the spring tour will provide a more tangible boost for the Wallabies. Coach Les Kiss confirmed Carter Gordon (broken leg), Hunter Paisami (suspension), Len Ikitau (concussion) and Ben Donaldson (groin) will all be good to tour, and Tom Hooper and Taniela Tupou will also rejoin the squad after stints with their clubs.

Advertisement

Halfback Ryan Lonergan conceded the confidence of the Wallabies had taken a “pretty big hit”, but said they’d been provided with “a good wake-up call” by the All Blacks about being clinical when given chances to score. The Wallabies had small windows to remain in the fight against the Kiwis, by scoring and building scoreboard pressure, but mostly failed to execute. Max Jorgensen scores the match-winner at Twickenham in 2024. Stan Sport “It’s a great challenge to be able to play the All Blacks twice. Now we know where we’re at,” Lonergan said. “You miss the mark a little bit against the All Blacks, they make you pay with the pace that they play at. We know that even through Super Rugby that if you’re a little bit off, particularly around that collision area, they can make you pay because they’re such good footballers.” Rennie conceded New Zealand had focused on winning the breakdown, to negate the effectiveness of McReight, who he rated as “the best in the world” at poaching and disrupting a team’s recycle speed.

Advertisement

Having either been targeted by runners to make a tackle (he made a team high 19 in Sydney and 16 in Auckland) or with arriving players cleaning him out, McReight failed to win a single turnover in Sydney, and two successes in Auckland amounted to nought given the All Blacks had the penalty advantage. “I didn’t really get too many clean opportunities to be fair. I tried to make a mess of it a lot of times,” McReight said. Of the many lessons learnt, Lonergan said an important one was being more clinical when on attack in the opponent’s quarter. Several try-scoring opportunities were either lost through poor skill execution, passing choices or just the ability to keep dominating contact. Related Article Exclusive

Australian rugby ‘We didn’t share the same values’: Rennie breaks long silence on his Wallabies axing “Previously this year, we’ve stayed quite patient and we’ve been really, really good down there in that zone,” Lonergan said. “The last couple of weeks, we’re just missing that execution a little bit. It’s as simple as a pass sometimes. Our structures down there in that zone haven’t changed much – credit to their defence. They’ve really sent the two into that contact and slowed our ball down.”

An international mining giant has taken its $38 billion pursuit of Australia’s largest gold producer directly to local investors, offering them the muscle to build a globally competitive gold behemoth and hoping their pressure will help force the board to the negotiating table. Executives from South African-based miner Gold Fields brought forward plans for an Australian investor roadshow last week, seeking to boost its profile and win over key fund managers after Western Australia’s Northern Star Resources rejected its takeover attempt as “highly opportunistic”. Gold Fields chief executive Mike Fraser has been meeting with Northern Star’s institutional investors across Perth, Sydney and Melbourne. Ross Swanborough Gold Fields chief executive Mike Fraser spent the week meeting with Northern Star’s institutional investors across Perth, Sydney and Melbourne, noting that there appeared to be widespread consensus on the “strategic logic” of the tie-up. Slides shown at investor briefings stated that combining the two companies’ projects in Western Australia would forge a new global gold production powerhouse in a “world-class province”, capable of rivalling Barrick and Newmont Corporation’s Nevada Gold Mines joint venture in the United States, and Agnico Eagle’s Abitibi hub in Canada.

Advertisement

If the takeover ultimately succeeds, the combined group would rank as the second-biggest gold producer globally, behind Denver-based Newmont. It would control eight of Australia’s 20 biggest gold mines – including Northern Star’s massive “Super Pit” in Kalgoorlie – and produce 4.1 million ounces a year of the precious metal. Northern Star’s Kalgoorlie Super Pit is one of Australia’s largest open-cut gold mines. Trevor Collens “Creating a truly competitive global mining gold major that is centred out of WA is something that’s quite compelling in our view,” Fraser said. In an interview in Melbourne, Fraser revealed that his discussions with Northern Star began more than a year ago after, Gold Fields acquired a 3.5 per cent stake in the company via its acquisition of Gold Road. While some investors are pressing Gold Fields to sweeten its bid after Northern Star rejected its initial shares-and-cash proposal for being too low, Fraser is urging the board to first hold talks with Gold Fields, agree to the merits of the tie-up and grant access to its books.

Advertisement

Related Article Updated

Gold Australia’s biggest gold miner rejects ‘opportunistic’ $38b takeover offer “Let’s agree [to] the strategic logic of it and align that this is something we want to pursue,” he said. “I think if we can then go in and do due diligence, firm up the value, then we can have a conversation around value.” However, Northern Star chairman Michael Chaney said the board maintained that Gold Fields’ proposal did not appropriately recognise the quality and long-term value of the company’s portfolio of high-quality, long-life gold assets in tier-one mining jurisdictions, and its growth profile. He said the company’s directors remained focused on acting in shareholders’ best interests. “This includes engaging with parties on proposals that represent value above what we believe Northern Star can generate as a standalone company,” Chaney said. “The Gold Fields proposal was not in that category.” Under Gold Fields’ initial offer, Northern Star shareholders would have received 0.3125 new Gold Fields shares and $7.25 in cash for each share they own. The bid valued Northern Star at $38.7 billion, a 22 per cent premium based on both companies’ share prices on the last trading date before it was lobbed.

Advertisement

Editor's pick Gold Getting married? There’s a new chart to check before buying a ring Northern Star’s shares are now more than 10 per cent higher than they were the day before news of the Gold Fields approach leaked. “At current market values, the Gold Fields proposal is now at a discount to Northern Star’s share price,” Chaney said. One of the top shareholders whose support Gold Fields is seeking to rally is US-based activist investor Elliott Investment Management, which has built a 6 per cent stake in Northern Star and has been pressuring the board to make sweeping changes. The hedge fund has criticised Northern Star’s sharemarket underperformance this year and urged it to consider a sale or asset divestments. Gold Fields’ attempted takeover of Northern Star follows a multi-year rally in gold prices, fuelled by intensifying geopolitical tensions, worsening inflation fears, erratic policymaking in the United States and an erosion of trust in the US dollar.

Advertisement

Gold, the precious metal prized by civilisations for thousands of years for its rarity and use in jewellery, tends to be most sought after these days by investors as a safe place to store wealth during periods of extreme financial uncertainty. Investors said the approach for Northern Star reflected the growing strategic appeal of gold miners. “Gold miners are back in favour,” Betashares investment strategist Tom Wickenden said. title: It’s the final weekend of Fringe – here’s what you shouldn’t miss
text:
Advertisement

This year’s festival has kicked off. Here, our writers take a closer look. See all stories .

CIRCUS

Na Djinang Circus | Ocker

Civic Hall Ballarat, until October 25 Five performers from First Nations-led company Na Djinang Circus navigate the crowd while delivering death-defying circus stunts in the middle of Fed Square. We turn back in time to a pre-colonial era as dramatic, otherworldly music plays in the background. The troupe roves through the crowd as if hunting, then gathers on a platform. The intimate audience of onlookers grows once the public realise that something is afoot. Na Djinang Circus show Ocker. Tiffany Garvie The choreography is dynamic, as the artists impressively run and tumble through people and across the stairs, doing lifts and climbing on one another. Embedding Indigenous knowledge in contemporary movements, performers emulate animals and cultural practices. They cleverly introduce props – a ladder and a trolley – carrying and manoeuvring them across the flat and cobbled surfaces of the square. They mount the ladder, balancing on its rungs like a tightrope or handstand-style, then lay it on the ground like train tracks to ride the trolley over it, as if it’s a raft sailing along the Yarra River. Surprising and ever-moving, this place-based show is an exhilarating watch.

★★★★★

Reviewed by Vyshnavee Wijekumar

Advertisement

CABARET

Darby James | Little Squirt

Ballarat Mechanics’ Institute, until October 24 Darby James in Little Squirt. Liv Morison In the depths of Melbourne’s lockdowns in 2021, Darby James clicked on a Facebook ad for sperm donation. The UK-born musical comedian premiered his one-man cabaret based on the experience at Melbourne Fringe 2023 as Spunk Daddy, and this week performed its 100th show at the same festival. Little Squirt is distinctly contemporary, wrestling with some of modern life’s heaviest dilemmas. Dressed as a seaman (say it out loud), James ponders the ethics of having biological children as a cis gay man, and what it means to have a legacy. The performer is a master of tone, somehow striking a perfect balance between ejaculation jokes and moving monologues, all with his tightly controlled vocals. The audience responds in kind, from raucous laughter to stunned silence. Tech issues on opening night mean that James is unplugged, adding an extra layer of intimacy to this already deeply intimate and thoughtful show.

★★★★★

Reviewed by Giselle Au-Nhien Nguyen

Advertisement

CIRCUS

Head First Acrobats | Lash Out Cabaret

Meat Market, until October 17 Hoops! Swallowing swords! Aerial feats! A sexy circus show powered by palpable femme energy. Lash Out Cabaret. Callan Harris Lash Out keeps the crowd entertained with sideshows, striptease and “slutty stuff”. The all-female dance troupe perform incredible acts of flexibility — morphing their bodies to writhe through hoops or in a net rigged from the ceiling. Flirting with danger, there’s a fire trick where one of the performers lights foam off parts of her body, getting audible amazement from the crowd. Wearing lingerie, another contorts her body while lying on her stomach, bringing her feet so they’re beside her face. They come together at different points like a girl group, performing coordinated routines. The pop soundtrack across the show also packs a punch, featuring Pass that Dutch by Missy Elliott and Machine Gun Fellatio’s Pussy Town. The MC for the evening at one point does a hilarious burlesque routine where she creates a balloon vulva while spitting facts about vaginas. Spectacular, sassy and sultry — Magic Mike can eat his heart out.

★★★★★

Reviewed by Vyshnavee Wijekumar

Advertisement

COMEDY

Creepy Boys | SLUGS

Meat Market, until October 17 This is Fringe at its purest – and this show comes with more content warnings than a film by Larry Clark. SLUGS was nominated for Best Comedy Show at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe last year, and rightly so. It’s delirious mayhem from Canadian artists S.E. Grummett and Sam Kruger. SLUGS is at Meat Market until October 17. Bokeh Media How often do you see the genitalia (some accompanied with googly eyes) of both performers, and see them threatening an audience member at gunpoint, then offering another a very raunchy sex service that can’t be printed in these pages? Free candy is also extended to the crowd, so it’s not all R18+ (but it is 99 per cent of the time). There’s deliberately poorly performed puppetry (shout-out to a terribly voiced Joni Mitchell), and the two cosplaying as a horse. Essentially, it’s Play School on crack with a decent dollop of existential doom and dread woven in. If you’re a fan of comedic chaos with the capability of warping your mind, then I couldn’t recommend it more highly. If you prefer your comedy more middle of the road and TV friendly, then stay far, far away. SLUGS is a paradox of a show. It’s advertised as being about “nothing, nothing, nothing, nothing, nothing, nothing, nothing, nothing” but is somehow about everything. It’s breathtakingly stupid but ingeniously clever. I never want to see it again, but I also want to book again for tomorrow night.

★★★★★

Reviewed by Tyson Wray

Advertisement

CABARET

Mara Knezevic | Kauboj

The Motley Bauhaus – Cabaret Stage, until October 11 In the hands of a master storyteller such as singer-songwriter Mara Knezevic, a simple tale about a Croatian man’s life and ambition becomes an enthralling and touching adventure. Two years after first staging Kauboj at Sydney Fringe Festival, the classically trained artist has brought her show to Melbourne. Kauboj by Mara Knezevic. Benjamin Draisma We hear about a chef-slash-cowboy named Jakov, who lives in the fictional Dalmatian town of Božje Selo. It’s a migrant story of hope and disillusionment. Through spoken word and song, Jakov’s world – brimming with purpose, love, fear and failure – is deftly and vividly created. Electric guitarist Daniel Potaczala strums along. Nostalgia and hints of humour are seamlessly woven in. Knezevic’s soulful, evocative vocals tackle a mix of traditional folk, covers and originals. Tender original tunes Till I See You Again and Cecilia’s Lullaby enchant, while we’re asked to sing along to an upbeat Kauboj Café and Grill. Professionalism reigns as stage lights flicker and falter and the sound plays up for a few moments. It’s a delightful hour that passes quickly.

★★★★★

Reviewed by Donna Demaio

Advertisement

THEATRE

In Bed With My Brother | Philosophy of the World

Meat Market, until October 3 Affectionately known as the best worst band ever, The Shaggs were a trio of young sisters from Exeter, New Hampshire, whose astonishingly inept songs were later reappraised as genius by the likes of Kurt Cobain and Frank Zappa. Philosophy of the World. Rona Bar & Ofek Avshalom That’s the official story, at least. Here, another trio reviews the legacy forced on three women who never wanted their spot in the limelight, but who were made to perform and record by a domineering father. In other hands, this material would lend itself to satire and condescension, but UK outfit In Bed With My Brother treats The Shaggs with respect while simultaneously trashing most conventions of respectable theatre. If you like your performances truly unpredictable, this is your ticket. Bristling with barely containable energy and randomly erupting into violence, music or comedy, the work suggests that to truly redeem artists with no aesthetic merit requires us to rewrite the rules of art itself.

★★★★★

Reviewed by John Bailey

Advertisement

EXPERIMENTAL

Freya Schack-Arnott | Nornir

Abbotsford Convent, season finished Nornir might be inspired by figures from Norse mythology, but its vision of life and especially death is harsh and distinctly modern. It places us somewhere between a giant dismantled cello and a prison or military camp, with spotlights and wires stretched between scaffolds. Nornir Darren Gill Cellist Freya Schack-Arnott and dancer Trà Mi Dinh enter slowly, faces hidden behind hanging hair, long limbs unfolding. There is, in fact, hair everywhere: torn loose, heaped up, snagged on wires. It drifts through the light. The historical echoes are profoundly disturbing. The amplified wires, violently strummed with clumps of hair and ragged bows, shriek and groan. And there are deeper resonances beneath. It’s primordial music, but not what Wagner dreamed for his three Norns. The music of fate here sounds like a death-psychosis. Eventually, at the cello, Schack-Arnott restores a sense of measure. The instrument is at first melancholy but articulate. The order, however, cannot hold, as Dinh continues to scrape at the wires. Soon the cello, too, lapses into the squealing speech of chaos and night. The rough hair-pulling and abused instruments seem to condemn the particular violence of femicide; but Nornir also encompasses, in the strange poetry of its composition, a more obscure, dark and unlovely truth of the world and its destiny.

★★★★

Reviewed by Andrew Fuhrmann

Advertisement

COMEDY

Stephanie Hare | I Hope They Call Me Skinny in the Eulogy

The Motley Bauhaus – The Cellar, until October 18 From the outset, Stephanie Hare reveals their sleight of hand: physical misdirection and witticisms delivered with the gentle bemusement of someone almost surprised to find themselves delivering punchlines to an appreciative room. Adorned in a black funeral dress, the significance of which grows plainer as the show progresses, Hare moves from their sheltered, off-grid upbringing in Tasmania to a relationship that takes them to Scotland. Stephanie Hare, I Hope They Call Me Skinny in the Eulogy. With a deftness that neither valorises nor romanticises a chronic illness at a time when thinness has been elevated to the pinnacle of feminised beauty, Hare traverses eating disorders, abortions and complex entanglements. Hare’s tremulous voice belies a steady command of the room and their material. The subject matter is heavy, the revelations often harrowing and astonishing, but therein lies Hare’s talent. They’re exceedingly skilled at building narrative tension, drawing unexpected connections that make fun without making light, and delivering bons mots with a pin-drop precision that’ll have you simultaneously guffawing and grimacing.

★★★★

Reviewed by Sonia Nair

Advertisement

THEATRE

Hani El-Rafei | The Bruise

The Motley Bauhaus, The Cellar until October 18 What if instead of you fighting the pain, the pain was fighting you? The Bruise is Hani El-Rafei’s pain incarnate, and it turns out his pain has the form of a Victorian dandy. The Bruise is a high camp, richly intense character with a hint of buffoonery, and he takes centre stage while El-Rafei, relegated to a portrait in the corner, attempts to psychically wrestle back control of his mind and body. Hani El-Rafei in The Bruise. Through the retelling of a series of Arabian fables from his grimoire, The Bruise makes his case that pain is a worthy teacher. He asks audience members what they learned from the stories, and they are, of course, hilariously wrong. A politician lauding the cultural cachet of Melbourne while refusing to bolster the arts sector in any real, tangible way? Tick. As the play lurches wildly from farcical hijinks to sincere proselytising about the role of art in a whiplash-inducing manner, it simultaneously lampoons itself and us while paying homage to its intended audience. Leftists too busy preaching to the converted and fighting among one another to organise. Artists making work centred on their latest diagnoses. Clowns.

★★★★

Reviewed by Sonia Nair

Advertisement

DANCE

Caroline Meaden | Immacolata

Chunky Move Studios, until October 3 Immacolata. Caroline Meaden, Jeff Busby and William McBride This is a beautifully strange and melancholy solo dance vigil: a restless choreographic grisaille, delicate and disquieting. Caroline Meaden struts and frets, with crisp bird-like movements, then hesitates. Always there is hesitation in this work. Then an arm – or a hand or a leg – begins to wobble. It’s like a part of the body just turns to water. The dimly lit stage is furnished with only a clothes rack, some biscuit crumbs and a stool, but Meaden keeps mostly to its edges. She is pulled backwards or drawn into the corners, as if kept out of the empty centre by some unseen force. Immacolata tantalises with the mystery of its significance. What does it all mean? Is there a story behind its troubling silences? In fact, Meaden provides an accompanying essay, intended to be read after the performance, which does explain much of what we see – and gives the work’s air of sadness a touching specificity.

★★★★

Reviewed by Andrew Fuhrmann



Advertisement

COMEDY

Kimmie Lovegrove | L.O.V.E = It’s in the name

Bard’s Apothecary, until October 17 Kimmie Lovegrove is a lover, not a fighter. How could she be anything else, with “love” right there in her name? This may be the case, but don’t mistake being a lover with being soft. The theme is love but the performer isn’t afraid to sprinkle in a dicey topic or two. The complications of being a Ngarrindjeri woman looking for love in Naarm provide plenty of opportunities for Lovegrove to add ample cheek to her natural charm. Kimmie Lovegrove, L.O.V.E = It’s in the name. Elena Burger-Guimaraes She has a laid-back confidence that sets a relaxed tone for the room and builds a good rapport with the audience. Spinning stories about share-house living, being a young black woman with six degrees under her belt and a weakness for dating white men, her tales are told with a keen eye for the humour in contemporary life. A born storyteller, Lovegrove easily wins the audience over and keeps them charmed throughout.

★★★

Reviewed by Lefa Singleton Norton

Advertisement

Frenzy Theatre Co’s Not Soooo Fresh Belle Hansen CABARET

Frenzy Theatre Co | Not Soooo Fresh

Trades Hall Common Rooms, until October 18 “Very Y2K, very in right now,” a character says in Not Soooo Fresh. That could be the tagline for Belle Hansen and Sarah Bowers’ one-two punch of nostalgia: the 2008 teen film Angus, Thongs and Perfect Snogging recreated, jukebox musical-style, to So Fresh Winter 2010. The commitment to the bit is admirable, down to the film’s iconic olive costume, but creative liberties are taken to make the setting distinctly Australian: protagonist Georgia (Luisa Scrofani) berates her friends for not dressing up as “Aussie hors d’oeuvres”, and dreamy brothers Tom and Robbie are imports from Mildura. Adding a meta twist, Hansen and Bowers oversee it all as themselves, pitching the show to Fringe.The concept falls apart by the end, and some songs performed are definitely not of the era – Natalie Imbruglia’s Torn would like a word. But despite this and some opening night blunders, the 15-strong cast and audience alike are having a ball during this silly, joyful hour.

★★★

Reviewed by Giselle Au-Nhien Nguyen

Advertisement

EXPERIMENTAL

JC the Guy | Taiwan Folk

Festival Hub: Meat Market – Craft Room, until October 17 As a showcase of Taiwan’s spirit of social activism, rich queer lineage and enduring cultural traditions, drag king JC the Guy’s four-act show Taiwan Folk succeeds on every level. Where it falters is in its execution. JC the Guy in his Melbourne Fringe Festival show Taiwan Folk. Dory Visio Video interludes akin to egregiously edited tourism infomercials charting different periods in Taiwan’s history demarcate each act. But the screen is positioned too low for many in the audience to see them, a comical misstep in a performance undergirded by an unbridled sense of chaos. The show careens wildly from a haphazard bamboo dance that almost takes out an audience member to a traditional Japanese-influenced number to the tune of cutesy 2017 viral hit Tokyo Bon (Makudonarudo) and voguing, sashaying and slut-dropping soundtracked by Todrick Hall’s I Like Boys – the last a particular highlight anchored by dancer Jason Chiu’s immense talent. JC swaps lip-syncing for singing in his affecting renditions of The Moon Represents My Heart, in honour of Taiwanese legend Teresa Teng, and rousing resistance anthem Island Sunrise.

Advertisement

The effect of so many tonal changes is discombobulating, not helped along by the motley crew’s vastly divergent dance prowess. JC’s immaculately choreographed, extravagantly garbed performances would go down a treat in a club, but the rickety stage in Meat Market’s Craft Room is more suited to a languid play than high-energy performances with rapid transitions and a full-ensemble dance crew.

★★★

Reviewed by Sonia Nair EXPERIMENTAL

Ben Noble | BE NOBLE OR DIE!

Wheat, Wine & Whisky, until October 18 Fringe is the festival for pushing boundaries and bending genres. Billed as a “game show”, this is essentially pub trivia with a twist – plus a sprinkling of experimental theatre. Ben Noble in his Melbourne Fringe Festival show Be Noble or Die. Noah Martin We find ourselves downstairs in a “bunker”, with Armageddon almost certainly upon us. Audience members are grouped into teams of four or more. If you haven’t come with teammates, fear not – this is a great way to meet new Fringe friends and bond over saving the world.

Advertisement

Noble presents some clever and thought-provoking framing devices, and delivers interesting on-theme trivia and interactive team exercises along the way. But for this to succeed as a paid one-hour event, it needs to lean far more heavily into its artistic instincts and away from a traditional trivia format. After all, people can get that at the pub next door for free – plus with drinks prizes up for grabs.

★★★

Reviewed by Hannah Francis Follow That Turtle! is at Theory Bar until October 18. Nick Dale COMEDY

Tegan Higginbotham | Follow That Turtle!

Theory Bar, until October 18 Staging a #MeToo show in 2026 could be construed as tired and dated, says Tegan Higginbotham, but have the fault lines exposed by the 2017 global social movement really been eradicated? We know they haven’t. Back doing stand-up after eight years, Higginbotham’s latest show revolves around the sexual harassment and intimidation she experienced in an unnamed corporate workplace. If something so heinous doesn’t sound funny, it isn’t, but much of what scaffolds it is. There’s the series of “your mum”-esque jokes, but about Higginbotham’s hairy husband, Paul. An unfortunate run-in with airport security services revolving around a certain piece of contraband.

Advertisement

Higginbotham is an animated, ever-confident performer aided by some excellent lighting design and audio interjections, but the storytelling can be muddled at times. Callbacks are aplenty but vary in their payoff. And the truths spouted at length about the need to stamp out misogyny, while spot-on, are too broad and self-evident to truly pack a punch.

★★★

Reviewed by Sonia Nair THEATRE

Jazzy Story | Smoko

Trades Hall - Music Room, until October 18 Smoko is at Trades Hall until October 18. Laura Seeds Beccy is a depressed small town horn dog, who just started a new job at the Alice Springs Dump. She lives at home with her dysfunctional parents, can’t decide if she wants to be more than just “emergency contacts” with the girl she’s seeing, and uses a lot of attitude to mask her bubbling depression. Everyone in Alice passes through the dump. Beccy’s life is examined through the multiplicity of voices: the chagrin from her co-workers, the rejection from her lover, and her mother’s callousness. Jazzy Story performs all the characters, save some cued-over audio. It’s an impressive one-woman show, demonstrating Story’s range as an actor, but the cacophonous cast means you don’t stay with a character long enough to care about them, which dilutes the show’s emotional impact.

Advertisement

The set is charmingly handmade, with hand-painted tapestries and milk crates for mountains. A highlight is the puppets, a hauntingly beautiful half skeletal dog running across the stage, a mottled seagull flapping its wings over the tundra of the landfill. It’s a poignant show with a lot of heart.

★★★

Reviewed by Rose Lu THEATRE

Tim Ellis | Darkness is Coming

The Laneway Theatre, until October 17 Drawing inspiration from the horror shows of the historic Grand Guignol theatre in Paris, this experimental theatre-slash-magic performance is not for the faint of heart. Darkness is Coming is at The Laneway Theatre until October 17. Lee Cohen Among the lengthy list of content warnings are the simulation of murder, self-harm, suicide and violence against women. But well-known Melbourne magician Tim Ellis is a master of his craft, and is able to harness this discomfort for the audience’s enjoyment. He manages to weave close-up magic tricks into the eerie overarching narrative of the show – all without uttering a single word.

Advertisement

The Laneway Theatre (which is in an undisclosed location, revealed upon receiving your tickets) is also part of the charm, down to the secret phrase you must utter into an intercom to gain entry. The performance at times dips into needlessly gory or overly eccentric territory, but there are enough twists that you’re constantly left wondering what’s to come.

★★★

Reviewed by Gemma Grant COMEDY

BS Productions | Improv RPG: Dungeons & Dragons

Trades Hall – Solidarity Hall, until October 11 A gnome, a dwarf and Elvis Presley walk into a tavern. This is all we know going into BS Productions’ Improv RPG: Dungeons & Dragons. The actors, it turns out, are just as clueless. Based on the popular role-playing game, this comedy show is entirely improvised. No script, no blocking, just basic character sheets and a Dungeon Master to guide the way. Improv RPG: Dungeons & Dragons. Yannick Douzals A gang of unlikely heroes must overcome the evil usurper king and replace him with the rightful monarch. But in improv, the story ultimately doesn’t matter. Major plot points are abandoned at will, and key emotional scenes transform into sexual romps in stables.

Advertisement

The show loses some momentum midway as characters separate, leaving fewer opportunities to riff off each other, but the ad hoc comedy and cobbled-together costumes feel endearing and deliciously awkward throughout. Whether you’re laughing at the occasional solid off-the-cuff joke or at its patchwork aesthetic, the point is you’re laughing. And that’s good enough.

★★★

Reviewed by Nell Geraets The Kentucky Meat Shower is at Meat Market until October 17. Alexandra Fimeri THEATRE

Alexandra Fimeri | The Kentucky Meat Shower

Meat Market, until October 17 Though it claims inspiration in a real event, this unhinged farce bears only the slightest resemblance to a world you or I might recognise. In 1867, a small town in Kentucky was pelted by unexplained meat from the heavens, and from that factoid playwright Alexandra Fimeri has woven a lurid spectacle of cannibalism, murder and a talking meat grinder with the face of a 16-bit video game toddler. It’s a little bit Crucible and a little bit Texas Chainsaw, all delivered with Monty Python silliness and hicksploitation irony. The humour and accents are equally broad, and while the jokes are occasionally and intentionally tasteless (pun also intended), they’re served up with the kind of bonhomie that goes with good ol’ Southern hospitality.

Advertisement

The folksy, handmade set and props crafted entirely from cardboard adds to the sense that this saga of savagery is meant not to turn the stomach but leave it pleasantly sated.

★★★

Reviewed by John Bailey Before We Begin played at Trades Hall. John Rata EXPERIMENTAL

Hamish Annan | Before We Begin

Trades Hall - Quilt Room, until October 11 If you’ve ever wanted to go on a bizarre group speed date, this is the show for you. Hamish Annan takes victims/volunteers from the audience on an escalating series of intimate interactions. Always with their consent first, of course. The tasks are revealed with a ding on the screen behind Annan. SHAKE HANDS. RIZZ. UNDRESS ME WITH YOUR EYES. They all relate to dating, specifically gay dating. SWITCH. POPPERS. The promotional image of a banana with a condom on it, like Chekhov’s gun, demands to be blown.

Advertisement

It’s a modern take on sex education, with Annan peppering tidbits about enthusiastic consent and intimacy co-ordination between tasks. The line between the sexy and the absurd is thin, and the show is at its strongest when crisscrossing over that line. The ending is a tonal shift into the serious and the personal, and one that, as Annan acknowledges, might be a bit heavy for a first date.

★★★

Reviewed by Rose Lu THEATRE

Emerson Brophy | Parasocial

La Mama Courthouse, until October 11 Ex-influencer Emerson Brophy sings about the subtle manipulations of parasocial online relationships in this fun musical theatre show. Brophy rose to online fame to build his music career – the pitfalls of being an artist in the content era. Through lyrics and dialogue, Brophy shares well-studied reflections on how he and other artists, such as Taylor Swift, built a brand of relatability with their followers for personal gain. Parasocial played at La Mama Courthouse. Darren Gill The tech set up is quite clever for a modest production. Live smartphone filming, equipped with a ring light, is projected onto a screen – flipping the lens on content creation. Brophy also performs an original boyband-style number alongside three different versions of himself onscreen, cleverly syncing up the harmonies. There is the occasional glitch, which is expected for a preview show, but Brophy’s affable style and improvisational flair enables him to glide past them.

Advertisement

The music numbers are aplenty, from emotive keyboard ballads to an Irish shanty, showcasing Brophy’s versatility. I found myself waiting for that earworm, but it never quite came. Being more sparing with musical numbers, and building up to them within the dialogue, would enable more standout moments and ensure the segues feel seamless. With some refining, Parasocial has all the makings of a topical hit show – consider me influenced.

★★★

Reviewed by Vyshnavee Wijekumar COMEDY

Oliver Pol | Featherbrained

The Motley Bauhaus, until October 11 Featherbrained. Ash Church Did you know that birds get drunk? Neither did I. But if you notice a silly goose flying in a wobbly motion and honking at strangers minding their own business in the park, it’s mostly likely because they just got on the sauce of naturally fermented berries and fruit. It’s one of the very obscure avian insights that New Zealander Oliver Pol found when researching this show from an article in an 1881 edition of The Lyttelton Times. Alongside his other ornithic anecdotes, Featherbrained at the very least makes a solid argument that he might be the only antipodean comedian more obsessed with birds than Geraldine Hickey. With manic and nervous energy, Pol pinballs through a myriad of feathered tales patchworked together with accounts from his adolescence through to adulthood. He graphically details getting botox (just not where you’d imagine injecting it), the anxiety-ridden workings of his OCD brain, his family’s history of cancer and how you can die from giving yourself a love bite.

Advertisement

There’s also fat to be trimmed. A conversation with the crowd about pen licences meanders along, as does a poll about whether he should grow a moustache and a similarly aimless observation of Spotify playlists. Nevertheless, it’s a solid enough 45-minute debut that just needs sharper polish in its delivery and a more structured throughline rather than a torrent of tangents. But if you’re looking for an affable newcomer to start off your evening, book (book) your tickets quack snap. ★★★

Reviewed by Tyson Wray COMEDY

Holly Bohmer, Mario Hannah and Taylor Griffiths | Nosebleeds

The Improv Conspiracy, until October 18 Nosebleeds is at The Improv Conspiracy until October 18. Simon McCulloch and Mario Hannah The Nosebleeds, veterans of improv comedy, know it doesn’t take much to evoke the horror genre, even less to make fun of it. The trio, together for a decade, are back at Melbourne Fringe to take a proverbial (and literal) stab at the evergreen genre with an hour of uneven but charming sketches. Exorcisms become blind dates, séances turn into couples therapy, and haunted mansions turn nipples into weapons. Rather than looking to recent films, the self-described “comedian cinephiles” pull from an older vintage of horror. It’s Mel Brooks via Henry James. Holly Bohmer is the perfect wide-eyed governess with no fear of her homicidal employer, Mario Hannah is the ever-likeable himbo contacting the dead to learn more about the Titanic, and Taylor Griffiths, who delivers the night’s best punchlines, is uproarious as every manservant with a handlebar moustache or ghost child.

Advertisement

But by the fourth Victorian-era conceit or ill-formed attempt at audience engagement, the show becomes static and its parodies rote. It’s a fun night out, but it’s not quite a scream.

★★★

Reviewed by Guy Webster THEATRE

Gregory Nussen | QFWFQ

Trades Hall, until October 4 In this brave dissection of self, politics and art, Californian performer Gregory Nussen takes their cue (and title) from Italo Calvino’s metafictional work, If on a winter’s night a traveller. Centre stage is a writer’s desk piled with Calvino’s extended works, and we continue through a series of false starts as Nussen keeps attempting the play they’re “meant” to perform. QFWFQ. Sonya Katerina It’s a neat framing device for their autobiographical narrative, in which the preordained script of a rigid Jewish upbringing creates visceral and lasting internal conflict for a protagonist whose sexuality and gender identity don’t stick to the script. The most powerful moments draw an elegant through line between the cognitive dissonance of war and propaganda (both historical and current), and the terrifying and complex pursuit of self-actualisation and truth in a world where, too often, two plus two continues to equal five.

Advertisement

There is plenty to like here, but the overall result is too many references and layers – some of them heavy-handed to begin with, then unnecessarily explained – which distract from its beating heart.

★★★

Reviewed by Hannah Francis VISUAL ARTS and FILM

Youbi Lee | OBANG 오방

ArtPlay, until October 25 If you’re accustomed to picking up after a toddler, this interactive visual arts experience will make you feel right at home. OBANG 오방 combines the Korean term for five, O, with the word, BANG, referring to direction or room. The minimalist space is set up as a halmoni’s (grandmother’s) house, with individual stations representing the kitchen, bedroom, toilet and living room, alongside a partitioned area for the bathroom. OBANG 오방 is at ArtPlay until October 25. Darren Gill Familiar household elements ignite sensory play: a mini kitchenette, a bed, a clothing line and a blow-up bath. Tactile elements feed curiosity: plastic puddle decals, a dumpling steamer, silk manchester, a straw hanging and a wooden puzzle. The experience is low stimulation, with gentle traditional music and a wall projection adding an audiovisual dimension.

Advertisement

The space is modest, which creates a safe and contained environment, but limits the number of families that can engage simultaneously, and the amount of time you can occupy an active toddler. As you leave, respect halmoni’s home by leaving the space as you found it, which is a good lesson for the young.

★★★

Reviewed by Vyshnavee Wijekumar Blak Out played at Trades Hall. COMEDY

Blak Out: An Indigenous Comedy Showcase

Trades Hall, until October 4 Blak Out is an ideal comedy show to see early at Fringe. It offers a range of performers delivering a taste of what they offer, leaving the audience hungry to seek them out elsewhere at the festival. The featured comedians hail from all over the country, and with a mix of four performers each night there is a satisfying variety of styles. When I attended, Wiradjuri/Kamilaroi performer Jacob Keed opened with a laconic storytelling style to ease the audience in, followed by Gamilaroi comic Ben Moodie. His material skewed darker with quick jabs that met their mark. Ngarrindjeri actor/producer/comedian Kimmie Lovegrove’s personal material offered a tempting preview of the material in her solo show, which will open later in Fringe.

Advertisement

Kamilaroi performer Cameron Ribbons, the MC for the evening and the closing act, stole the show on this night by hitting a sweet spot of storytelling and punchy jokes. His re-enactment of crocodile spotting was the perfect crescendo.

★★★

Reviewed by Lefa Singleton Norton DANCE

Weichen Cui | In Green, In White

Dancehouse, until October 3 The Chinese folk legend of Lady White Snake is forever shedding one skin for another. The most recent retellings shift the focus from White Snake’s mortal lover to her demonic servant, Green Snake, recasting the bond between mistress and maid in terms of enduring female friendship and homoerotic desire. In Green, In White. Georgia Moloney Choreographer Weichen Cui explores this queer transformation in a new duet with Jiawen Feng. At first, the performers are silhouetted behind separate screens, isolated, wearing costumes informed by tradition. As if reflecting the evolution of the story, the two figures are gradually brought together – culminating in a final serpentine tangle of limbs.

Advertisement

There are interesting moments, such as the use of waacking to playfully disrupt a fan dance. But overall, the episodic structure feels slow and over-formal, arresting the flows of desire it seeks to release. It might also be a little long – compressed to half an hour, this duet could bring its strongest moments into more volatile contact.

★★★

Reviewed by Andrew Fuhrmann DANCE

Joyce Liu | INTERLINK_SYSTEM

Dancehouse, until October 3 Joyce Liu stands before us in the gloom, a tangle of red wires trailing from one arm, fingers twitching. Finally, we get it: she is actually controlling the soundscape, summoning jackhammer bursts and ominous bass drones from a body that barely seems to move. As the noise intensifies, four creatures wake inside a plastic greenhouse behind her. They claw at its walls, tearing them open. Free at last, the juddering young humanoids – all in their underwear – begin feverishly coupling in a sort of grotesque orgy-of-Doctor-Moreau. INTERLINK_SYSTEM. Carlin Stephenson Liu – also director and choreographer – builds a convincingly creepy laboratory atmosphere, with smoke and wildly sweeping lights lending urgency to the action. There’s also some irony, even comedy, in the monstrous debauch – though it does go on and on.

Advertisement

I do think, however, we could have stayed with that opening image of the human wired for sound a little longer, perhaps giving the idea of an interlinked system more room to unfold – before rushing into the bioengineered bacchanal.

★★★

Reviewed by Andrew Fuhrmann THEATRE

Ben Grant | Wrong Way, Grow Back

La Mama Headquarters, until October 18 Wrong Way Grow Back channels long-time actor, Ben Grant’s warm-hearted charm and boyish sincerity for a part-stand up, part-confessional reflection on family lineage, memory, and grief. The title names Grant’s stop-and-start style of delivery, as he swings from mournful anecdotes about his parents’ meet-cute at Harvard to light-hearted stand up about the romance of letter-writing. Ben Grant in his Melbourne Fringe Festival show Wrong Way, Grow Back. Darren Gill

Advertisement

He’s an endearing performer. But the show lacks focus. Though the scattershot logic of Grant’s stream-of-consciousness style has an occasionally charming unpredictability (an uncanny Louis C.K. impression notwithstanding), it’s too much to ask even the most game audience to go from twee word play to sermonic political rants with nothing but the refrain “Why was I telling you this?” to justify the diversion. If there’s a chaotic appeal to Grant’s jarring transitions, it comes at the expense of the simple effectiveness of moments when he draws from his talents as a dramatic actor to deliver something closer to the intimate style of confessional or verbatim theatre: whether quietly reading from his parents’ letters to each other, or choking up when he tries to make a joke about his mum. The simplicity of these moments of quiet vulnerability stripped back the clutter to present a process of painful remembrance unique to grief, where two lines on an old letter can stop time and let you ‘grow back’. At least for a moment.

★★

Reviewed by Guy Webster COMEDY

Gill Cordiner, David Callan and Iain Pringle | 100% Scottish Comedy

Elephant and Wheelbarrow, until October 16

Advertisement

100% Scottish Comedy is at Elephant and Wheelbarrow until October 16. Brian Taylor Three Scottish stand-ups pull a decent-sized comedy-seeking crowd for a Monday night. There are 30 or more people thirsty for a laugh at the bustling inner-city pub. David Callan welcomes “Monday drinkers” before launching into a diatribe about how crappy Perth is. He seeks validation from the crowd, revealing he’s trialling new bits. While some chuckles surface, many quips and observations get the silent treatment. Next is Iain Pringle, whose attempts at an Aussie accent elicit mild mirth. Again, Perth is bagged out. After the half-way mark, he notes, “I’m definitely losing you on this”. Ramblings about working for the NDIS entertain some. Gill Cordiner’s fun crowd banter leads to light-hearted ribbing of prime targets – a bald bloke, a man wearing a hat indoors and a younger fellow with facial hair. Oddly, there’s even more rubbishing of Perth. A highly relatable dig at Melbourne’s foodie scene gets the biggest laugh of the night.

★★

Reviewed by Donna Demaio The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

title: Sam Pang is the most popular man on TV. Now what?
text:

The last time I clapped eyes on Sam Pang in the flesh was in the media room backstage at the Logies, just minutes after he’d been anointed the most popular person on Australian television. “How are you?” he says today as we settle in to talk about the return, for a third season, of his variety show Sam Pang Tonight. “Last time we spoke you were front row, and one of the first people I saw post-Gold Logie.” Well, you know, Sam, it’s important to share these moments with the people you love ... “I did point that out,” he says, laughing. “You walk offstage, you’re taken to this room, and you’re like, ‘this is who I’m celebrating with?’ It’s a very special moment.” Loading Don’t be fooled by the trademark sarcasm: it really was a special moment for Pang. As he said on stage and again backstage that night in August, he grew up watching TV and the Logies, but never dreaming that a kid who looked like him (which is to say, of Chinese descent) might one day be part of the industry, let alone walk away with its top prize. The whole experience was “crazy and weird and surreal” he says. When his name was called out, he was surprised – “it could just as easily have been anyone else” – but at least winning made the decision not to drink on the night feel worthwhile.

Advertisement

“That would have been a big sacrifice to make: to keep yourself mildly tidy on the off-chance [you win], and then not have to say anything,” he says. Pang didn’t drink in the three years he hosted the Logies either. But any time he’d been there as a guest, he says, “I absolutely gave it a genuine crack – I’d make friends with the waiter: ‘Help me out here, it’s a long night.’” Editor's pick Opinion

Australian TV If you are still complaining about Australian TV, it’s time to shut up Louise Rugendyke National TV editor And what about when he woke up on the Monday morning with the gold statuette on the bedside table? Did it feel as if the world had suddenly shifted on its axis? “I don’t think it’s changed anything workwise,” he says. “On the Sunday I was at the Logies, on the Wednesday I did The Front Bar, and the following Monday I did Have You Been Paying Attention? With the hosting, it was always like a poisoned chalice; [you fear] you’re never going to work again. [With this] I was thinking, unless this is a genuine disaster, I think The Front Bar will have me back. I think HYBPA will have me back. I felt comforted by that.” One of the more curious aspects of Pang winning the Gold Logie is that it’s not entirely clear which network should claim the bragging rights. Is it Seven, for The Front Bar? Ten, for HYBPA and Sam Pang Tonight? Or the ABC for Ground Up, the scripted comedy about the AFL’s efforts to launch a team in Tasmania? ‘I’m very aware of doing too much … But I always defend myself with, “Yeah, OK, well which show do you want me to get rid of?” ’ Sam Pang

Advertisement

“I’m definitely no network star,” Pang concedes. He just got lucky by being part of teams on a couple of shows in The Front Bar and HYBPA that started small and eventually found their way to longevity and a decent-sized audience (it should be noted that he’s also been on SBS and Fox Sports; only Nine has not yet claimed a piece of Pang). “I feel very lucky not to be part of that old system of network stars, or signed to one network. I feel very lucky that I kind of missed all that,” he says. Josh McConville (left), Emma Harvie, Dylan Murphy, Sam Pang and Lucy Durack in ABC comedy Ground Up. As in its first two seasons, in early and late 2025, there are only eight episodes of Sam Pang Tonight. That’s both strategic and necessary, given his other commitments. “I’m very aware of doing too much, and I know already there’s a bit of, ‘Hey, you’re on a lot of shows,’” he says. “I always defend myself with, ‘Yeah, OK, well which one do you want me to get rid of?’ “The other thing is, they are seasonal. There’s crossover, but I’m only on TV twice a week. Some people are on TV five days a week. And Ground Up was very separate.” Ten might have been open to a longer run of the variety show, “but I think this is just what it is at the moment”, Pang says. The idea of doing a full-time late-night show could not be further from his mind.

Advertisement

Sam Pang: “I never understood that model [of American late-night show].“: “I never thought about this show as like an American tonight show, 11 o’clock every night, five nights a week. I never understood that model – I didn’t know who was even watching television at 11 o’clock at night. It’s mind-blowing to me.” Related Article Opinion

Trump's America Colbert takes final bow, a casualty of the president who couldn’t take a joke Bill Wyman Contributor At any rate, that model is under threat in the US right now, both economically (as live audiences dwindle, so does the ad revenue) and politically (thanks to Trump’s ongoing war against anyone in the media who dares to criticise him). In Australia, it’s been extinct since the five-nights-a-week juggernaut Tonight Live With Steve Vizard ended in late 1993. Pang’s iteration of the format has more in common with Rove McManus’ one-night-a-week shows Rove and Rove Live, which ran in 1999 (a single season on Nine) and from 2000 to 2009 on Ten. But even there, there are differences. For a start, there’s less reliance on big-name international guests. It’s a necessary adjustment given that Hollywood junkets have become rarer than hen’s teeth since COVID. “If you’re in New York or in LA, on the off-chance that no one is publicising something, all the big stars live there so you can just ask a favour, say, ‘Can you pop down the street?’” Pang says. Pang with Rachel Griffiths, Sam Campbell and Russell Crowe.

Here, while guests are definitely still part of the mix, you have to approach the format a little differently. “It feels more like a variety show: this is my hour, I’ve got this awesome team, and this is what we’ve got for you. That’s a nice structure.” Ten is promising the new season will be “stacked with Monday monologues, uninhibited celebrity interviews, sketches and the anything-could-happen energy of Wheel Of Segments”, just like before. There will be guest announcers roped in from the world of comedy too, a role filled in the past by the likes of Shaun Micallef, Celia Pacquola, Tony Martin and Denise Scott. It’s an impressive roll call, and as with Ed Kavalee’s star-studded crime caper, Cop This, also made for Ten, it points to a sense of fraternity among local comedians. “I definitely feel part of a community,” Pang says. “I never thought I’d get to be a part of it, but I feel it. You hear stories about comedians, especially stand-ups, being very competitive and angry and bitter and cynical. I do not feel that at all. There’s a lot more support than people may think. It’s definitely a community, and I feel very lucky to be a part of it.” As for the show itself, Pang says lessons have been learnt from seasons one and two. “The DNA of the show is the same, but things have changed,” he says, highlighting a need for more bodies, more ideas. “It feels like we can just colour it in more, with more silliness and fun.” He also feels he’s growing as an interviewer: “I’ve learned to take my time a bit more and try to explore, not just get through these bits.”

title: The Greens are facing a run of tests in Shoebridge’s first weeks as leader
text:
IN BRIEF The challenges for Shoebridge started almost as soon as the 11-member party room chose him as its leader.

He is facing a range of issues, from allegations against party members to the party's Ukraine policy.

Three weeks into the job, Greens leader David Shoebridge has gone from a public row over Ukraine to criticism from his own colleagues and now an inquiry into one of his senators.

Since Shoebridge was elected leader of the Greens at the end of September, he vowed to "beat down One Nation" and expose Labor's "failures".

Instead, the story has been one of ill-contained disarray, with one crisis tumbling into the next.

Political scientist Zareh Ghazarian of Monash University's School of Social Sciences told SBS News that the past weeks had been catastrophic for a party under new leadership, which had struggled to make ground amid the rise of One Nation.

"This could not have been a worse start to Senator David Shoebridge's leadership for the Greens," he said, adding that the Greens had needed an opportunity to stand out in a "positive way".

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"That opportunity was there with a new leader, but these events and internal disagreements have taken their toll. It's been a very tough start to Senator Shoebridge's leadership."

'A real test'

The latest challenge came on Wednesday, when WA Greens senator Jordon Steele-John took leave from the party as allegations related to his comments about women triggered an inquiry.

While Steele-John "utterly" rejected the characterisation, which he said tried to "assert" him as someone he wasn't, the Sydney Morning Herald reported that the WA Greens branch had allegedly maintained a crisis communications dossier, instructing staff how to comment on any allegations made about Steele-John's conduct around women, for a decade.

WA Greens has said in a statement that it considers "any allegations of this nature to be serious and concerning" and that the "matter needs to be resolved via a fair, timely and independent investigation".

Ghazarian said the allegations "have the potential to destabilise the party and have a significant negative impact".

READ MORE Shoebridge pressed on what Greens knew after Steele-John investigation ordered

"This is going to be a real test," he told SBS News.

"Senator Shoebridge came into the leadership with a reputation as an effective communicator and parliamentary performer. He will need to draw on all of those skills.

"Ultimately, this is going to be a real test of his leadership."

Shoebridge has refused to say whether the party will publish the findings of the inquiry into allegations against Steele-John.

He also said he was unaware of past complaints about the senator until a letter from seven Greens members landed on his desk this week.

A 'destabilising' debate

The controversy around Steele-John came just days after the party reportedly faced internal disagreement over its policy on military aid to Ukraine.

In an interview with the Sydney Morning Herald during his first week as leader, Shoebridge said, "we don’t support military aid to Ukraine", while the party also "oppose Russia’s illegal invasion".

The stance drew criticism not only from other politicians and the Ukrainian community, but also from a high-profile party member.

Sarah Hanson-Young, the party's Senate business manager, who lost the leadership contest to Shoebridge, told ABC's 7:30, "We need to be doing everything we can to support the people in Ukraine".

When pressed on whether that includes providing military equipment, she responded, "If that's the support that people need in order to defend themselves from the invasion of Russia, I think Australians need to support that."

About 70 per cent of Australians support providing military aid to Ukraine, according to a poll by the Lowy Institute.

Ghazarian said the "debate about Ukraine has been destabilising for the Greens".

"They need to explain their policy positions clearly and be on the front foot when it comes to discussing public policy.

"Instead, they seem to have been on the back foot ... It is a very testing period for the Greens and for the new leader."

'Deep' internal divisions

The challenges for Shoebridge started almost as soon as the 11-member party committee chose him as its leader, after winning the party's first contested leadership ballot.

He beat former deputy leader Mehreen Faruqi seven votes to four, and Hanson-Young was knocked out in the first round.

In response, Faruqi said she was "disappointed the party room chose another direction" and that "many others will feel the same way", signalling possible divisions in the party.

In a video on social media, Hanson-Young also said: "God, politics can be brutal".

"The Greens have always had two broad strands within the party," Ghazarian said.

"One has been more focused on pragmatism and working with other political parties within parliament to achieve policy outcomes. The other has been more activist in its approach, with a stronger focus on changing grassroots behaviours and actions.

"Like other political parties, the Greens have internal divisions, and they can potentially be quite deep."

At the federal election, the party lost ground and has struggled to regain momentum, losing three of its four lower house seats — including the Melbourne seat held by its then-leader, Adam Bandt.

Now the Greens seem to have been overshadowed in the public debate by the attention focused on One Nation.

Ghazarian said the upcoming Victorian state elections in November "will be a significant test for the Greens brand".

"This is occurring at a time when the Victorian Labor Party appears to be losing support, the Coalition appears to be gaining support, and One Nation is also polling strongly," he said.

"This election will be a real test.

"Any faltering by the Greens could prove costly because it is always difficult to win seats back once they are lost."

title: The Bali venues taking a stand against bad tourist behaviour
text:
IN BRIEF Locals are reporting a rise in bad behaviour by tourists on Bali.

Bali was Australia's top holiday destination last year, with over 1.6 million people travelling to the island.

Shirtless diners, feet on chairs, arrogant tones and speeding motorbikes — a growing number of restaurants have "really had enough" of these bad tourist behaviours in Bali and are now taking action.

It's gotten so bad that Herzza Rahmadhani Duha, the owner of popular restaurant OUFFF in Canggu on Bali's south coast, told SBS Indonesian she's had to put a set of rules on the venue's door.

"If they don't follow the rules, they will be asked to leave immediately."

OUFF is one of several venues in Bali that have announced their expectations of guests on social media, coming together to make a statement.

It comes as locals report a rise in bad tourist behaviour on the island.

"Over the past year, I've seen an increase in rude behaviour from guests," Rahmadhani Duha said.

"This is not only happening in our restaurant, but also in other places across Bali, where tourists take advantage of the hospitality of Indonesians who genuinely try to welcome them warmly.

"They exploit that hospitality and do not repay it with kindness and respect."

'You are not welcome here'

Bali was Australia's top holiday destination last year, attracting more than 1.6 million travellers, according to the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade.

In September, an Australian tourist was deported after allegedly being caught on CCTV engaging in a sexual act in a residential driveway.

READ MORE The awkward new rules about to kick in for travellers to Bali

Rahmadhani Duha said she believes there is "one main reason" for bad tourism behaviour in Indonesia.

"Indonesians are very kind, perhaps even too friendly. People like this would probably not behave the same way in Europe or Western Europe. But here, they feel they can do whatever they want because Indonesians are too accommodating," she said.

Della Terra has said people riding scooters dangerously will be unwelcome. Source: Supplied / Della Terra

Other restaurants have also taken a similar stance against bad behaviour on their social media pages.

"If you ride dangerously in our neighbourhood, or your motorcycle has a modified or loud exhaust, you are not welcome here," DELLA TERRA, a restaurant at Pererenan, just north of Canggu, has posted on Instagram.

Restaurants against dangerous driving

Motorcycle and scooter accidents are very common in Bali, where many tourists prefer to rent a motorcycle. In 2024, the Bali Regional Police reported 142 traffic accidents that involved foreigners.

In recent years, local authorities have announced plans to restrict motorcycle access for tourists,

Openhouse cafe in Pererenan has partnered directly with the village council to fight against dangerous driving in the area.

Instagram post Openhouse cafe, Pererenan, Bali. Credit: Supplied

The cafe posted on Instagram that if guests are "caught speeding" by their cameras, they "will not be invited back" to the business "for life".

"If you feel the need to speed around the roads in the local community, you can go somewhere else; in fact, just leave the island," the post says.

Benn Nilsen, the Australian owner of the cafe, said that he has seen a few incidents building up "over the last year or so".

"A lot of people were messaging us because they were fed up with the behaviour. We realised that we have a responsibility. We're not trying to undermine the local government," he said.

"We simply have a platform, and many people don't feel safe or are having issues, and we felt we had to stand up for them. So we decided to make the statement."

title: 'It was an honour': Katie Zacharia breaks silence after White House firing
text:
In brief Katie Zacharia has been dropped as White House press secretary after less than a week in the job.

On top of a poor first briefing and questions over her legal credentials, she also mocked China.

Katie Zacharia has said she wished more Americans appreciated United States President Donald Trump, in her first public statement since she was forced out of her White House secretary role after less than a week in the job.

In a statement posted on X, Zacharia said it was an "honour" to work with Trump, who she described as a "kind, wonderful, gracious, thoughtful, enthusiastic, and hardworking man".

"I wish more Americans appreciated him," she wrote.

"No one will ever make America great the way he has and continues to."

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Zacharia was "let go" and was "transitioning out" of the press secretary position, according to reports from two separate White House officials.

It was a brutal close to her tumultuous five-day stint in the high-profile role, which included a series of public blunders that added to distractions for Trump.

She faced days of questions ‌about her legal credentials and criticism of her performance in a news briefing and interviews.

"Can confirm", a White House official told the Agence France-Presse news agency, after Fox News reported that Zacharia, 41, was "transitioning out".

The writing was on the wall earlier when Trump made clear he was ready to see his newly minted spokesperson go.

"I said, 'Katie, is this for you?'" Trump told reporters. "I said, 'Katie, you don't have to do this'... I said to her, 'Honestly, if I were you, I'd reconsider.'"

Zacharia only began her job five days ago, taking over from the combative Karoline Leavitt, who helped Trump reshape White House coverage by bringing in more friendly outlets and fiercely attacking critical media.

Zacharia had got off to a rocky start with her debut press room briefing Tuesday morning.

It lasted less than 15 minutes, beginning with a remarkably slow reading out of what she said were Trump's many accomplishments — then taking just three questions from journalists.

She then was plunged into controversy when it emerged that her previous claims to be a lawyer were not true.

The kerfuffle is a distraction for 80-year-old Trump as he flies around the country trying to boost Republican candidates ahead of the 3 November congressional midterm elections, with polls predicting a drubbing.

The Republican leader himself also faces ever-lower polls as Americans sour over the war against Iran, inflation and perceptions of corruption.

Controversy over Zacharia's legal credentials

Zacharia had described herself as a lawyer during television appearances and on social media, and listed herself as general counsel of a California-based conservative nonprofit.

While she does have a law degree from a California university, she acknowledged Thursday she had failed the bar exam, a prerequisite for practising law in the US.

She embarked on a series of damage-control interviews on Trump-friendly outlets, but they did no good.

In one of them, Fox News' Sean Hannity, a close Trump ally, appeared dismissive of Zacharia.

He asked the press secretary if she ever retook the bar exam. She replied: "I did not."

"It was never my intent to go into the practice of law," she said.

In another interview Thursday with pro-Trump outlet Real America's Voice, Zacharia said she had registered to take the bar exam but was "distracted and overwhelmed" by plans to move to China with her husband.

Zacharia said "many people in the field" had assured her that she could "label myself a lawyer," given her law degree.

Press secretary's potty-mouthed remarks

"Fox and Friends", which often conducts friendly interviews with Trump administration officials, was unusually direct on Saturday when a host asked Zacharia if she still had the confidence of the president.

"I hope to be able to build the trust and confidence of everyone around me," she said, sidestepping the question.

Zacharia further stirred controversy on Thursday when she disparaged China, whose leader Xi Jinping was recently Trump's guest in a pomp-filled Washington visit.

The press secretary recalled the perception in 2016 was that China would soon overtake the US.

"I remember this very distinctly, having just come from China, thinking: 'How is China the next country on the horizon? They don't even have proper toilets,'" she told right-wing influencer Jack Posobiec in an interview.

Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning responded Friday that Zacharia should "visit China more often".
