title: 'Life and death': What's at stake for diaspora communities as Israel heads to the polls
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

Nirit Eylon immigrated to Australia 21 years ago. This month, for the first time, she’s flying back to Israel specifically to vote.

The country does not allow citizens living abroad to vote from outside its borders.

But with an election many view as the most consequential in its history fast approaching, estimates from the US-based Fly&Vote initiative, which helps facilitate their travel, suggest as many as 53,000 Israeli expats are expected to return.

Eylon is among them.

"There is a perception that this election is about right and left. I don't believe it's so. I believe it's between right and wrong," the 52-year-old, who lives in Melbourne, tells SBS News.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Eylon believes Israel is at a crossroads. She views the election as a contest between competing visions of the country’s future: one grounded in liberal democratic values, and another shaped by religious nationalism.

She believes Israel's leaders must be held accountable for failures surrounding the October 7 attacks, and that political change is necessary for Israel to begin to heal.

Nirit Eylon says this election is about preserving Israel’s democracy and making a change so the country can heal from October 7. Source: Supplied

Eylon is far from alone in viewing this election as pivotal.

Israeli political science expert Shahar Burla, a contributing editor at The Jewish Independent, is one of more than 11,000 Israeli-born people living in Australia.

He tells SBS News he knows around 20 people in his immediate circle who are planning to return to Israel for the election — a circumstance he describes as "very unusual".

"I think that the main motivation is fear," he says.

There is a fear that if the Netanyahu bloc will win again, that will be the end of Israel as we know it as a democratic, liberal, free state.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government has pursued sweeping changes to Israel's institutions, including moves to curb the judiciary’s oversight of government decisions, while pushing increasingly hardline policies towards Palestinians and expanding Israeli military operations across the region, including in Lebanon and Iran.

Ongoing geopolitical tensions and fractured alliances mean the election will be watched closely by many outside Israel too.

SBS News has spoken with nine people from Jewish, Israeli, Palestinian, Lebanese and Iranian communities in Australia about what is at stake for them in this election, as conflict continues to reverberate across the Middle East.

While their views on peace, security and coexistence vary, they share one common belief: that Israel cannot continue on its current path.

For Palestinian Australian academic Shamikh Badra — who lost his father, his brother and his brother’s family to the war in Gaza — a change of government would be welcome, but he cautions it's not a simple fix.

"I am not saying that [the] next government will automatically be better, but removing this government is the first step," he says.

The electoral landscape

Netanyahu, as leader of the Likud party, has served as Israel's prime minister for nearly 20 non-consecutive years since he was first elected in 1996.

In the lead-up to the 27 October election, a relatively new, centrist party called Yashar has been polling neck and neck with Likud.

Former Israel Defense Forces (IDF) chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot leads the party, which takes its name from the Hebrew word for 'straightforward' or 'honest'.

Figures are based on an average of the latest polls published by Israeli television channels 11, 12 and 13, compiled by Haaretz.

Eisenkot is Netanyahu’s primary challenger to lead the country, and has a personal stake in Israel's ongoing conflicts, having lost both his son and nephew in the Hamas-Israel war.

He's running on a platform of accountability for the October 7 attack, promising to restore trust in Israel's institutions and strengthen national security.

Some of the big names in Israeli politics. Source: Supplied

But neither party is close to winning enough seats for a majority in Israel's 120-seat parliament, the Knesset.

That means coalition-building will be crucial to forming government.

Currently, Israel’s parties are divided over their willingness to govern alongside Netanyahu rather than splitting along traditional left-right lines. Two distinct camps remain: those willing to join a Netanyahu-led coalition, and those who may be willing to join one led by Eisenkot.

But neither bloc appears to have a clear path to a parliamentary majority, raising the prospect of political deadlock.

Burla notes that while Eisenkot has positioned himself at the political centre, his prospective coalition spans the political spectrum and includes right-wing parties.

That limits how far a new government could go on issues such as recognising Palestinian statehood and negotiating territorial compromise.

Among Israel's major Jewish-led parties, support for Palestinian statehood remains limited. Yair Golan, leader of the left-wing Democrats, is the only major party leader to have endorsed a future two-state solution.

Burla believes changing Israel's leadership could remove a "first obstacle" to peace with Palestinians, but does not expect significant progress in the coming years.

"None of them will speak about a Palestinian state at this stage, or any territorial compromise with the Palestinians.

"But I think that Eisenkot has at least the potential, the political potential, to move forward some kind of a peace process."

High stakes for those with a vote — and those without one

Yasmeen Abu Fraiha is a medical doctor who works with humanitarian missions in the Middle East.

She's one of roughly two million Palestinian citizens of Israel, a group that makes up around 20 per cent of the country’s population.

Fraiha tells SBS News many "feel the urgency in these elections". She believes Palestinian voters will turn out in higher numbers than they have for previous polls.

Palestinian citizens of Israel have historically voted at lower rates than the wider population. In the 2022 election, just over half of Arab and Druze voters cast a ballot, compared with more than 70 per cent nationally, according to the Israel Democracy Institute.

During a recent visit to Australia, Yasmeen Abu Fraiha found hope in Aboriginal land acknowledgements — something she says she can "only dream" of back home. Source: Supplied

Fraiha, too, feels democracy is at stake. But for Palestinians, she says, the consequences are more fundamental.

"I don't know if it will be necessarily better if [Netanyahu] loses, but it will definitely be worse if they win again," she says.

It’s really a matter of life and death for us as Palestinians, for sure in the West Bank and Gaza, but also inside Israel.

Yet many Palestinians who will be directly affected by the election’s outcome will have no say in it.

Badra, the Sydney-based researcher and community organiser from Gaza, says his family paid the ultimate price under Israel’s current government. His priority is to see it removed from power.

Beyond that, a path to peace will not be easy. But Badra says any lasting solution must address Palestinian rights and security, including an end to occupation and settlement expansion.

"Security for Palestinians means being able to live in your home without fear of bombing. It means children have food, medicine, education. It means people being able to move freely and live with dignity," he says.

Shamikh Badra says a new Israeli government should be "judged by its policies and what it actually does towards Palestinians". Source: Supplied

"It also means real political and human rights for Palestinians."

On 7 October 2023, Hamas killed 1,200 people and took another 251 captive during its attack on southern Israel.

Israel's retaliatory bombardment of Gaza has decimated much of the strip and killed more than 74,000 people, including more than 1,400 since a ceasefire began last October, according to the local health ministry.

The humanitarian conditions in Gaza remain dire, with critically limited access to food, water and essential services. UNICEF estimates nearly 84 per cent of Gaza’s population continues to live in overcrowded displacement sites or damaged shelters.

Far from Israel, but close to home

The election’s outcome will be felt far beyond Israel. For many Australians like Sam Hoballah, the results will be deeply personal.

Born in southern Lebanon, in a town close to the Israeli border, the Sydney-based interpreter moved to Australia 40 years ago.

However, much of his family still lives in Lebanon, a country scarred by civil war and decades of regional conflict.

As a child, Hoballah says he grew accustomed to periods of recurring war and insecurity. Last August, before Israel launched its ground invasion of southern Lebanon, he returned to his hometown to visit family.

"This time it was different," he tells SBS News of the conflict in recent years.

"While [they] have been living in a difficult, insecure situation in that part of Lebanon, this time it is catastrophic."

Sam Hoballah grew up several kilometres from the Israeli border with Lebanon.

Following the Hamas-led attacks on Israel on 7 October 2023, a new chapter began in the decades-long conflict between Israel and the Lebanese militant group Hezbollah.

Despite a ceasefire in November 2024, the conflict flared again in March this year, after Israel and the US initiated war with Iran.

The Iran-backed Hezbollah fired rockets at Israel in support of its ally, triggering a major Israeli air and ground offensive in Lebanon.

READ MORE Inside Lebanon's war zone where medics are targets too

More than 4,300 people have since been killed in Lebanon, according to the country’s health ministry, while dozens of Israelis have been killed in the conflict.

Israel’s occupation and bombardment of southern Lebanon has flattened villages and displaced hundreds of thousands of people.

Hoballah says his own siblings are among them; parts of his hometown, Shaqra, have been reduced to rubble.

"It's a total misery there now," he says.

"So you can imagine the psychological impact this has on our community here [in Australia]."

The 66-year-old says he can’t recall a time in his life when people in southern Lebanon felt safe under any Israeli government.

"To be honest, there was some differences, but no major difference."

He has little faith the election will bring meaningful change, but hopes to see Israel led by a more moderate coalition.

I'm a person who believes that people of different nationalities, race, faith, they can live together, and we can live with the people in Israel.

For Australians with ties to Iran, the war has also brought Israel's political future into sharp focus.

Suren Edgar, vice president of the Australian Iranian Community Alliance, says the conflict has affected many in his community very personally.

"You are consistently checking the news, trying to contact people and worrying about what may happen next," he tells SBS News.

He says decisions made by Israel’s next government "could have direct consequences" for his friends, family and the wider region.

"For me, what is at stake is whether the region moves toward another cycle of war, or towards greater stability."

Edgar hopes Israel's next government will balance its security concerns with the need to protect civilians and infrastructure, recognising that long-term security cannot come from permanent regional conflict.

Iranian Australian Suren Edgar believes lasting regional peace will be difficult to achieve while Iran’s government remains in power. Source: Supplied

"I hope it understands that weakening the Islamic Republic and weakening Iranian society are not the same thing."

Across different diaspora groups, the election is also being viewed as a vote on the direction the country will take in managing its foreign relationships and conflicts into the future.

Ric Benjamin is chair of the New Israel Fund Australia and a longtime organiser within Australia’s Jewish community.

He says many Jewish Australians feel "strongly connected to Israel" and are passionate about its elections, even if they can’t cast a ballot.

Benjamin points to the work of Jewish and Palestinian Israelis who continue to cooperate despite the conflict, such as those in the health and humanitarian sectors, as a rubric for Australians navigating their own divisions.

Israeli Australian Limor Fayena says the path to peace is difficult to imagine after October 7, but she believes it’s possible. Source: Supplied

"If it's possible for people who are on the ground in the conflict, who have on both sides lost people through war or terror, if they are able to come together, why is it that our communities, 15,000 kilometres away, can't find that when they cry out for help?

Let's focus on the common causes and the common issues we have, and through that build trust and and build an acceptance.

That desire to break the cycle of conflict at the ballot box is one of the reasons Israeli Australian Limor Fayena has extended her trip to Israel. It will be her first time voting in Israel in 20 years.

The Sydney-based 50-year-old software engineer, who is also Burla's partner, says she hopes her vote will help bring about a "more responsible government" — one that will consider the future being created for the nation's children and grandchildren.

"How can we minimise the option of another war and sit down and think about the future — not the current and not the past?"

text:
For Australian-born rugby league player Jordan Samrani, the upcoming World Cup match between Lebanon and Papua New Guinea is significant — not only is it his international debut, but it's also his first test match representing his ancestors' birth country.

Samrani is in PNG, preparing for his international debut as Lebanon's Cedars face the PNG Chiefs in the Rugby League World Cup on Saturday.

Speaking with SBS News, Samrani said it was a "real privilege" to represent Lebanon, his grandparents' homeland.

"Australia has given our families everything, and we're very grateful for that. But when you get the chance to represent your homeland, it's a real privilege.

"When you get the chance to represent your homeland, you're really representing your family and your heritage," he said.

The 24-year-old, who plays for Sydney's Parramatta Eels, was selected to play for Lebanon in the 2019 Rugby League World Cup 9s, but at 17, he was blocked from playing because he was under the NRL age limit of 18.

A team with an Australian flavour

Lebanon's World Cup campaign has a strong Australian flavour, with Australian coaches Michael Cheika, former Wallabies coach, and Matt King, recently appointed New South Wales Blues State of Origin head coach, leading a 23-man squad — of which around 20 players are attached to Australian clubs.

"We're all grateful to live in Australia," Samrani said.

"Our grandparents came from Lebanon seeking a better life, so Australia has given our families everything."

The team's assistant and kicking skills coach is Nick Davis, a former Sydney Swans player known for bringing home the premiership in 2005, and former Wallabies star Will Genia joined the support staff as a liaison officer and skills trainer for this weekend's opener against Papua New Guinea.

The additions complete a team with a long-standing connection to Australia — the Cedars were formed by Lebanese Australians in 1997.

Samrani said that while it was his debut for Lebanon, he'd already had a "great" time around the camp, and that making connections had been "much easier" in an environment of shared cultural background.

"We're Australian, but our heritage and ethnicity are Lebanese," he said.

"When you're with people from the same culture, who share similar values and family backgrounds, the connection comes much more naturally."

'Unreal' fans in PNG

Samrani said the fans had been a key highlight of his time in PNG, where Rugby League is the national sport.

"The fans here have been incredible — they're chasing down our bus and asking for Lebanon jerseys," he said.

"It's unreal to see."

The whole team was really excited to embrace the PNG fan base and culture, Samrani said.

"It's going to be a great atmosphere, and I don't think you get to experience anything like this back home."

He said the culture around PNG's energetic fan base would differ from Lebanon's, but that didn't mean the Cedars had any less support.

"Most people in Lebanon probably don't know what rugby league is, but they see the cedar on our chest and know we're representing Lebanon.

"We're all proud to represent Lebanon and our families. We don't just do it for ourselves, we do it for everyone."

title: Australians were getting this vaccine for free. Now they could pay up to $180
text:
IN BRIEF: There is no national set price for private COVID-19 vaccines, with prices varying across pharmacies.

Experts have said that, while costs could deter some, at-risk populations should be the priority.

Australians could now pay anywhere up to $180 for a COVID-19 vaccination, depending on which pharmacy they attend, with one retailer telling SBS News it was unlikely to stock it at all.

On 1 October, the COVID-19 vaccine was moved into the routine National Immunisation Program (NIP) schedule, replacing the standalone National COVID-19 Vaccine Program established during the pandemic that offered free jabs.

While the NIP will continue to cover the cost of COVID-19 vaccinations for at-risk cohorts, such as older Australians and severely immunocompromised people, those who are ineligible will have to pay an out-of-pocket cost to get the jab.

With no nationally set price, vaccination providers have discretion to set costs for those ineligible under the NIP.

SBS News identified significant price differences across Australian pharmacies, with one TerryWhite Chemmart outlet charging $120 while consumers were paying $179.99 at Chemist Warehouse stores Australia-wide.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

A spokesperson from Priceline Pharmacies told SBS News that, as each of its outlets was independently owned and operated, the decision to offer COVID-19 vaccinations and set their prices was made on a store-by-store basis.

One Priceline store in Sydney's CBD quoted the private cost of the vaccine at $130.

Another in the Melbourne CBD said that, while they weren't currently offering the vaccine for people not covered by the NIP, they were expecting to charge a price similar to Chemist Warehouse's $179.99.

Another nearby Priceline store said that, due to the wholesale cost, it was unlikely to stock the private vaccine.

A spokesperson for Terry White Chemmart wasn't available to comment, but SBS News identified that prices for the shot across the chain's locations ranged from $120 in Melbourne CBD to $170 in central Adelaide.

No national set price or requirement to stock

Anna Theophilos, who owns a TerryWhite Chemmart pharmacy, told SBS News that the high wholesale price for the private vaccine meant pharmacists would make "business decisions" based on demand, including whether to stock the vaccine.

Theophilos, who is also the inaugural national vaccination ambassador at the Pharmaceutical Society of Australia, said minimum order requirements and the expiration date of current stock were key issues.

"The current vaccine has a short expiry date of February, which is contributing to the hesitation," she told SBS News.

"Usually we have a longer expiry date and pharmacists have agreements with wholesalers to ensure suppliers can buy back expired stock."

She said an agreement between wholesalers and pharmacies regarding expired stock would be the "final piece that comes into play".

Australia 'can't provide every vaccine free'

Under the NIP, the COVID-19 vaccination is available for free to adults aged 75 and over every six months, and adults aged 65 to 74 every 12 months.

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people aged 50 to 74 also remain eligible for an annual dose, as do adults aged 18 and over who are severely immunocompromised.

University of New South Wales School of Population Health professor Holly Seale said that, while the price of a private COVID-19 vaccine might deter some Australians, the decision to move it onto the NIP was the right one.

She said it would align Australia with other countries and ensure people who most needed the vaccine received it as part of a broader package of adult vaccinations.

"The government has to assess who is most at risk and where vaccines will have the greatest impact," she told SBS News.

"We can't provide every vaccine free of charge, nor do we need to."

READ MORE The COVID trend Australia wasn't expecting this winter

Seale said the decision prioritised those more likely to be hospitalised, and was based on available evidence and international data.

New vaccines are in development that could see two vaccines combined, for example COVID-19 and flu, that could mean the cost of an individual vaccine is reduced, she said.

"We are in a transition phase, but I think there are lots of new developments happening around the COVID vaccine that we just have to wait for, and see what happens."

The latest respiratory surveillance report shows that only 8 per cent of Australians received a COVID-19 vaccination in the past year, compared with the influenza vaccine at 30.5 per cent.

Cost was reported as a barrier by about a quarter of people who experienced difficulty getting a flu vaccine, according to Australia's National Vaccine Insights Survey.

Theophilos said it "would be naïve to say the price won't deter some people".

"Of course it will. But I think it will ultimately come down to people understanding their individual risk and whether vaccination is recommended for them."

Australians 'lagging' behind new vaccines

Earlier reporting from SBS News revealed that the latest COVID-19 vaccine tailored for new variants remained unavailable in Australia.

Pfizer and BioNTech's latest COVID-19 vaccine, adapted to target the XFG subvariant, was approved in the United States for the 2026-27 season, following international guidance to more closely match vaccines with contemporary circulating variants.

While Australia does not yet have that formulation registered, Seale said it wouldn't be the main factor affecting vaccine uptake, adding that Australia had managed similar strain updates with influenza vaccines for many years.

"There are a lot of factors involved in vaccine procurement and supply. Just because an updated vaccine becomes available internationally doesn't mean it's immediately possible to secure enough doses locally," she said.

Pfizer and BioNTech's LP.8.1-adapted COVID-19 vaccine was registered on the Australian Register of Therapeutic Goods in late 2025 and became available in Australia in December.

Moderna's LP.8.1 formulation has also been registered in Australia.

A 'positive step'

While the private COVID-19 vaccine rollout was still in its early stages, Theophilos said she was pleased to hear reports of customers undeterred by the new price.

"Australians place a lot of value on their health, and sometimes we underestimate that. People who are proactive about staying up to date with recommended vaccinations may still choose to receive the vaccine despite the cost," she said.

"It's something we'll need to assess once people actually have the opportunity to purchase it."

Seale said it was important to recognise that moving the vaccine onto the NIP was a "positive step" that ensured coverage was targeted toward those who needed it most.

"If people do feel they're at risk, or if there's an increase in cases in their community, they still have the option to purchase the vaccine privately."

title: 'Asymmetrical social warfare': Kelly Clarkson, a mechanical bird, and store put 'in danger'
text:
In Brief A dispute over a mechanical bird has snowballed after duelling claims and accusations of online harassment.

A New York toy shop says Kelly Clarkson's complaints sparked abuse and put staff "in danger".

A singing mechanical bird named Molly has become the unlikely epicentre of a public dispute between singer and television host Kelly Clarkson and a small novelty store in New York.

What began as a shopping trip to a Brooklyn toy and magic shop has since escalated into a fight involving competing Instagram statements, leaked CCTV footage, accusations of online harassment, and claims staff have been put "in danger".

It's also, somehow, left the world's "most famous" singing bird with a new US$15 million ($21.4 million) price tag.

The saga began when Clarkson visited Art of Play — a toy, games and magic shop in Brooklyn.

Among the items on display was Molly, a handcrafted singing and dancing animatronic bird mounted on a wall inside the shop.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Not long after leaving, the Grammy-winning singer made a post on X claiming she'd felt judged by staff while trying to make a purchase.

"Just drove all the way to Brooklyn to check out this store I thought looked really rad and had a few things in mind to buy and literally was looked at as if I couldn't afford it," Clarkson wrote.

Clarkson compared the experience to a famous scene from the film Pretty Woman, in which Julia Roberts' character is dismissed by sales assistants in an upmarket boutique.

"Y'all should go check out Art of Play in Brooklyn if you enjoy being treated like Julia Roberts' character in Pretty Woman," she said.

Kelly Clarkson's visit to a Brooklyn toy and magic shop has sparked a viral dispute over an animatronic bird.

At the centre of the disagreement was Molly, which Clarkson says she wanted to buy despite the item's US$15,000 ($21,400) price tag.

"[I] was told he could find something comparable for me," Clarkson said.

"Wow, dude. You're an idiot and just lost a huge sale."

Molly 'not for sale', store says

Art of Play disputed Clarkson's version of events and said there had been a misunderstanding.

In a statement posted on Instagram, the store said Molly was never available for purchase because she served as a mascot and fixture of the store.

"Molly is permanently attached to the wall and isn't for sale," the store said.

The store later expanded on that explanation, saying staff told Clarkson that, while Molly was not for sale, a similar bird owned by the automaton's creator, Seattle artist Bliss Kolb, could potentially be purchased for US$15,000.

Art of Play also said staff offered to show Clarkson another mechanical bird made by a German clockmaker that sold for about $2,000 ($2,860)

"She did not stick around long enough to see it," the business said.

Clarkson subsequently disputed that account, saying staff had explicitly told her Molly was for sale.

"So the whole conversation we had when I asked you if it was for sale while pointing to the price tag hanging on the wall with the title Singing Bird didn’t happen as you elevator-eyed me saying in a condescending tone, 'Yes, it’s for sale, but it costs $15,000 so if you’d like me to find something comparable for you, I can'," she wrote on X.

Clarkson said she regularly supports small businesses, but argued that "you don’t get a free pass to treat people less than in your store just because you are a small business".

The dispute took another turn after podcast host Pablo Torre obtained and released CCTV footage from inside the store, depicting Clarkson wearing a yellow shirt and a baseball cap.

The footage, which contains no audio, appears to show Clarkson browsing items, pointing towards Molly and speaking with staff.

After the exchange, Clarkson appears to put items she was carrying back on a shelf before leaving.

According to Torre, Clarkson spent less than five minutes inside the store.

Because the footage has no sound, it does not resolve the central disagreement over what was said.

'Kelly Clarkson has put us in danger'

As the dispute spread online, Art of Play said it was overwhelmed by the reaction.

"Imagine our surprise when our small local business was suddenly attacked by 8 million people who have never visited our store," it said in an earlier statement.

The store later said it hoped it could "clear things up" with Clarkson.

Store co-owner Adam Rubin has since accused Clarkson of directing unwanted attention towards the business.

"We are afraid for the safety of our shopkeepers," Rubin told reporters outside the store.

"Kelly Clarkson has put us in danger."

Rubin described the backlash as "asymmetrical social warfare" and later told radio station 1010 WINS there had clearly been a "miscommunication".

He said the attention had become overwhelming and that staff had turned off the store's phones.

The concerns escalated this week when a man filmed himself outside the store yelling expletives and accusing staff of "racially profiling" Clarkson.

"We feel no ill will against Kelly Clarkson," Rubin said. "We invite her to come back and enjoy the store."

Where is Molly now?

Molly is still hanging on the store's wall, seeing much more foot traffic than usual, and sporting a much higher price tag.

Following the dispute, Art of Play replaced the original $15,000 sign with a new price tag, listing Molly for US$15 million ($21.4 million).

Art of Play's store owners said they told Clarkson that Molly, pictured being installed by its creator Bliss Kolb, was permanently attached to the wall and was not for sale. Source: Supplied / Art of Play / 69Atlantic

The sign describes Molly as the "world's most famous singing bird automata".

Whether anyone buys her remains to be seen.

title: Shoebridge pressed on what Greens knew after Steele-John investigation ordered
text:
In brief A Greens senator has stepped aside as allegations trigger a probe.

An independent process will examine a letter containing allegations related to comments about women.

Greens leader David Shoebridge has refused to say whether the party will release the findings of an inquiry into allegations against Greens senator Jordon Steele-John.

Steele-John,32, has rejected allegations that he made inappropriate comments towards women and has taken leave from the Greens party room.

Shoebridge denies he knew about historic complaints about the Western Australian senator between 2017 and 2025, until a letter from seven Greens members demanding an investigation into "concerning behaviour" landed on his desk this week.

"I've been leader now for two weeks, and when I received these complaints, I took the most timely action that I believe you could take, and I'd ask people to judge me and on the response that’s been taken, the timely response that's been taken," Shoebridge told reporters on Friday.

"This is a process that will be commissioned by the WA Greens, and the parameters that we are very clear about is it will be fair, and it will be independent, and it will be timely. But it is not my role to put parameters around what we have said must be and will be an independent process.

title: 'Inconsequential': Trump's new press secretary confirms she didn't pass the bar exam
text:
In brief Donald Trump's new White House press secretary has said the results of her bar exam were "somewhat inconsequential".

She said she moved to China shortly after graduating and "knew I wouldn't need the bar in China".

White House press secretary Katie Zacharia appeared to confirm on Friday that she did not pass a United States bar exam, following mounting questions over her legal credentials days into her new role.

Zacharia had repeatedly presented herself as a lawyer during media appearances, and US President Donald Trump described her as "an attorney" when announcing her appointment last week.

However, journalists found no record of her being licensed to practice law in any US state, spurring questions about how she had represented herself.

The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday, citing a source familiar with the matter, that Zacharia sat the California bar exam after graduating from Pepperdine University's law school in 2011 but did not pass.

Obtaining a law degree does not automatically qualify someone to practice law. California's state bar confirmed to US media that it had no record of Zacharia holding a license under either her married or maiden name.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Appearing on the right-wing Real America's Voice network on Friday, Zacharia said she had been in a long-distance relationship during law school and moved after graduating to be with her husband, who worked at an American private equity company in China.

The 41-year-old said she had pre-registered to take the bar but was "distracted and overwhelmed and excited" to be married.

"The results are somewhat inconsequential because I knew I wouldn't need the bar in China and we left shortly thereafter," she said, without explicitly stating if she had passed or failed.

"After moving to China, I think I didn't really think much of the bar results or consider that something that I needed to focus on, and I was offered a job at an international practice division of a Chinese law firm."

"There's no Chinese bar. I had enough credentials — which was my law degree — to be able to do this practice."

Foreign nationals cannot sit China's bar exam. However, they can undertake certain legal work at Chinese law firms.

Zacharia acknowledged there was controversy over her decision to present herself as a "lawyer" but branded it "misinformation" and "miscommunication".

She said she had consulted "many people" in the legal field and determined she could call herself a lawyer, but not an "attorney at law" or "Katie Zacharia, Esquire". She said she'd been advised she could provide legal analysis but not advice.

"It’s unfortunate that people dub this as some kind of conspiracy or want to put me in a camp," she said on Real America's Voice.

"The truth is ... I was very careful how I executed this, and I never came across as someone who was an attorney-at-law."

According to a CNN investigation, Zacharia shared at least 15 social media posts, such as those from Fox News and other news segments, identifying her as an "attorney" over the past two years.

A tumultuous first week

Zacharia, a devotee of Trump's right-wing MAGA movement, was not well known to the public before she was elevated to the country's most prominent podium.

Her first briefing, which lasted just 15 minutes, featured praise of Trump and a stumble in which she accidentally referred to the president instead of her husband.

She took just three questions, all from organisations considered to cover Trump favourably: Fox News, the right-wing website Breitbart and the Daily Mail.

Zacharia previously served as an adviser to Trump Media and Technology, the group behind the president's Truth Social platform, and as a legal adviser to conservative group Fix California, according to a LinkedIn profile.

Katie Zacharia seemed to suggest she passed a bar exam in China earlier in the week, sparking further confusion. Source: Getty / Win McNamee

Before taking on the White House role, she frequently appeared on conservative media outlets Fox News and Newsmax.

In response to initial questions and reports about Zacharia's legal background, the White House said Zacharia "moved to China with her husband after graduating because of his job at an American private equity firm while she worked on international transaction law".

Within days, a US watchdog group had filed a complaint with the State Bar of California, asking it to investigate whether Zacharia had broken the law by repeatedly presenting herself as a lawyer without a license.

Campaign for Accountability said Zacharia had described herself as a lawyer during television appearances and listed herself as general counsel of a California-based conservative nonprofit.

"Ms Zacharia has represented herself as a lawyer repeatedly to buttress her reputation and credibility," said the group's executive director, Michelle Kuppersmith.

"The State Bar should investigate whether Ms Zacharia has misled the public about her credentials," she added.

Zacharia said in a statement to the media that she had "practiced international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials".

When a reporter asked on Tuesday in which state she passed the bar exam, she appeared to reply: "when I moved to China".

title: It's a risk in some of Australia's favourite destinations. Now there's a vaccine
text: In brief Heading to Bali or another tourism hotspot? A new vaccine may change how you prepare for your trip. Here's what to know about dengue fever, where the risk of contracting it is highest, and how it can be mitigated. Some of the most popular travel destinations for Australians are also places where dengue is common. Prevention has traditionally relied on avoiding mosquito bites. But with the dengue vaccine Qdenga now available in Australia, travellers have another way to protect themselves. Deciding whether to get vaccinated isn't always straightforward. Here's what you need to know. What is dengue? Dengue is a viral illness spread by mosquitoes. It typically causes fever, headache, body aches, nausea and rash. News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS. There is no specific treatment. Most people get better in one to two weeks, but for some, fatigue can persist for weeks or months. Some people will develop severe illness and need hospital care and, in some cases, dengue is fatal. There are four types of dengue virus. Infection with any type can make you sick. After infection, you're protected against that type in the future, but can still be infected by the other three. A second infection with a different type can sometimes cause more severe illness than the first. The reasons are complex, but one is that antibodies left over from the first infection can make it easier for the new virus to infect cells. People who live in, or frequently travel to, places where dengue is common are more likely to be exposed to different dengue virus types over time. Where is the risk highest? Although mosquitoes that can spread dengue are found in tropical parts of central and far north Queensland, local dengue outbreaks are now rare thanks to a successful public health program involving the release of mosquitoes infected with a bacterium that blocks the spread of viruses. For Australians, the main risk is during overseas travel. More than 1,900 dengue cases were reported in Australia in 2025, largely in returned travellers. Between 2012 and 2022, Indonesia, Thailand and India were the most common places Australian travellers got dengue. Some popular destinations for Australians, such as Bali, have frequent outbreaks. Dengue can be more common at certain times of year, and outbreaks can cause case numbers to rise sharply from one year to the next. The risk in many regions is also increasing as a changing climate creates more favourable conditions for the mosquitoes that spread it. Why has developing a dengue vaccine been so difficult? A dengue vaccine needs to protect against all four virus types and not increase the risk of severe disease if someone gets infected with dengue after they have been vaccinated. An earlier vaccine, Dengvaxia, was found to increase the risk of severe dengue in some children who had never had dengue before, and then got dengue after being vaccinated. That experience means new dengue vaccines have been closely studied and assessed for safety. How well does Qdenga work, and is it safe? Qdenga uses weakened dengue viruses to teach the immune system to protect against all four types of dengue virus. It is given as two doses, three months apart. Millions of doses have now been given worldwide, and an increased risk of severe dengue has not been seen following vaccination. In a large study of children and teenagers living in countries where dengue is common, the vaccine prevented about 80 per cent of illness and more than 95 per cent of hospitalisations in the first year. Protection against hospitalisation remained high for more than four years. READ MORE The common viral infections that are responsible for one in eight cancers Like all vaccines, Qdenga can cause side effects. In recent European studies, around half of travellers receiving Qdenga reported side effects, most commonly pain or redness where the injection was given, headache, fatigue or muscle aches. Most were mild and lasted one to three days. There are still some gaps in the evidence. Most studies looking at how well Qdenga prevents dengue have involved children and teenagers. Studies in adults have focused more on immune responses and safety than on directly measuring protection against dengue. Among people who have never had dengue, Qdenga provides strong protection against types one and two, but there's more uncertainty around protection against types three and four. As a result, different countries have made different recommendations about who should receive Qdenga. Qdenga also isn't suitable for everyone. Because it is a live vaccine, people with weakened immune systems cannot have it, and it's not recommended during pregnancy. So, should I get vaccinated? Getting vaccinated isn't a simple yes-or-no decision. Advice may differ depending on where you are going, whether you have had dengue before and how much exposure you are likely to have in the future. A discussion with a health professional can help you decide whether vaccination is right for you. In Australia, Qdenga is recommended for travellers aged four or older who have had dengue before, and for those who haven't but expect to spend a long time, or make repeated trips, to places where dengue occurs. It costs around AUD$300 for two doses. For someone who hasn't had dengue and is only taking a shorter trip, the decision is more individual. Factors such as where you're going, how long you'll be there and whether there is a current outbreak can all influence whether vaccination is worthwhile. What else can I do to avoid dengue? Whether or not you get vaccinated, avoiding mosquito bites remains important. Aedes aegypti, the main mosquito that spreads dengue, tends to bite during the day, often around the lower legs. Travellers should use insect repellent outdoors during the day. It's a good idea to buy it before you leave, as products available overseas may not be tested to Australian standards. Wearing loose-fitting long pants and covered shoes can provide extra protection. Bed nets can also help if you're sleeping during the day, particularly somewhere without insect screens. title: The growing issue that could make migrating to Australia less attractive
text:
IN BRIEF: Australia's unemployment rate is currently 4.7 per cent.

An expert says if it rises people may be deterred from coming to Australia.

Australia needs a strong labour market to attract skilled migrants, an expert says, as the unemployment rate hovers above expectations and is expected to rise.

The Australian Bureau of Statistics said on Thursday Australia's unemployment rate for Australia in September was 4.7 per cent — the highest it's been since October 2021.

The August rate was initially flagged as 4.6 but revised up to 4.7.

It's expected to rise over the next two years, as the government and Opposition have all sought to reduce net overseas migration (NOM).

The International Monetary Fund forecast unemployment in Australia would climb by 0.3 per cent, from 4.4 per cent on average this year to 4.7 per cent next year, at which point the number of Australians out of work would approach 800,000.

Economics and public policy commentator Abul Rizvi told SBS News a weak labour market would turn away not only migrants, but also Australian citizens.

"What you will see is an increase in departures and reduction in arrivals," he told SBS News.

But Rizvi said the unemployment rate in Australia would have to rise "much more significantly" for there to be the kind of "exodus" that was seen in previous years, including during the 1990-1991 recession.

Coalition migration approach 'illogical'

Rizvi has questioned the federal Coalition’s migration target, saying it doesn't take into account labour market factors.

The Coalition's migration plan, released last week, vowed to get NOM down to 100,000 — slashing temporary migrant visas, student visas and bridging visas, while increasing the number of skilled visas by 100,000.

Speaking on ABC's Insiders program on Sunday, Opposition leader Angus Taylor argued Australia's migration system should be focused on attracting workers with skills that increase productivity, rather than relying on population growth to drive economic activity.

"We are reducing the numbers and raising the standards," Taylor said.

"Because we are raising the standards, raising the incomes and tax paid of people coming into this country, that can be budget-neutral.

READ MORE The surprising health condition some people develop after moving to Australia

Rizvi said the Coalition's plan was "illogical" and avoided discussing the state of Australia's labour market.

"The Coalition wants to do two contradictory things at the same time," he said.

"They want to reduce the level of NOM, which requires a much weaker labour market. At the same time, they want to increase the level of skilled migration, which requires a strong labour market.

Labor plans to cut NOM down to 225,000 by 2028, focusing heavily on "visa hopping", international students, backpackers, and bridging visas.

One Nation plans to cap visas at 130,000 per year, which it says will ease pressure on housing, wages, and infrastructure.

A 2021 Treasury paper estimated each skilled migrant provides a $198,000 benefit to the Australian economy.

They generally arrive in the country after finishing their education, while the average Australian costs the budget $85,000 across their lifetime because they receive more money back in services than they pay in taxes.

Motivations for coming to Australia

As debate continues over migration policy, analysis from libertarian think tank, the Centre for Independent Studies released this week, found that economic and job opportunities were the top reason first generation migrants self-reported for coming to Australia, and that their motivations differed greatly from what Australian-born citizens expected.

The next most common reason the report found was cultural factors, such as the Australian lifestyle, values and customs, while Australian-born citizens were much less likely to assume this as a motivation for migration.

The data on 3,552 voters across Australia found that new Australians were far less likely than Australian-born citizens to say that access to a strong social safety net or welfare was important to migrants’ decision to come.

It was a similar picture for the Australian environment, with 31 per cent of new Australians saying factors such as the weather and cleanliness were a reason for migrating, compared with what 11 per cent of Australian-born respondents thought.

Skill mismatch

Successive studies have found that even during times of economic strength, it was difficult for migrants, and especially refugees, to find appropriate work in Australia.

Research from public policy think tank the Committee for Economic Development of Australia, found nearly a quarter of permanent skilled migrants in Australia were working in a job beneath their skill level, or experiencing a "skill mismatch", which was at a substantially higher level among migrants on Family and Humanitarian visas.

It also found that, on average, recent migrants earned significantly less than the Australian-born population, across all temporary and permanent visa types.

In the Scanlan Foundation's 2026 Multiculturalism in Focus report, published in February, nearly half of interviewees reported that securing meaningful employment was their greatest challenge after arriving in Australia.

Common barriers included non-recognition of overseas qualifications and the disadvantage of lacking local work experience.

Migration’s boost for local workers

Migration has been found to reduce unemployment for domestic workers in international studies, including a 2025 study on OECD countries that found a "significant" negative relationship between net migration rate and the unemployment rate of Australian-born workers.

The report found that Australia demonstrated well-planned immigration approaches through active selection methods, accepting professionals with high qualifications while providing integration assistance to new residents.

Australia’s economy could absorb increasing numbers of migrants while still providing employment opportunities for both Australian-born workers and immigrants.

A series of OECD reports published from 2023 to 2024 also found that Australians of all ages and genders benefited from migration, which boosted the labour productivity and employment of Australian‑born workers.

The Sydney Marathon has introduced guaranteed entry for local runners for the 2027 race under one condition; they have to have completed at least 10 prior Sydney Marathons. While once a measly 3000 or 4000 people ran in the event, popularity has surged, particularly in the past two years after the marathon was granted world major status. Now more than 123,000 people enter the general ballot for 40,000 places, with Australians vying for a spot on the startline against runners from 139 other countries. Viv Kartsounis is a member of the Sydney Marathon Bridge Club. Wolter Peeters The Sydney Marathon has long recognised the group of just under 100 runners who are members of the Bridge Club. That club consists of athletes who have run at least 10 previous Sydney Marathons as members. Before this year, the benefits of being in that club involved little more than some free merchandise and having their names enshrined on the event website. There was no need for a guaranteed entry before the race was afforded major status because there was no risk of missing out on a place at the North Sydney starting line.

Advertisement

But the surge in popularity has meant even Bridge Club members started missing out. In response to their dismay last year, race organisers said they were revising their ballot for 2027 and now, 100 spots have been set aside for Bridge Club members ahead of the general ballot closing on Monday. Because the club’s membership is currently less than 100, all will be guaranteed a spot for the 2027 race, which will be run on Sunday, August 29. It’s a privilege that had previously only been extended to an even more exclusive club of six runners, known as the Blue Line Legends, who have run every race since 2001. Competitors in the 2026 Sydney Marathon. Getty The guaranteed entry has been years in the making for the race’s most loyal runners. “You would be side by side with your friend at the start until the world major started,” Viv Kartsounis, 62, said. Kartsounis has run 16 Sydney Marathons. “But now you have to understand it’s a world major. It’s a huge event.”

Though Kartsounis has been able to bag a spot in the two years in which the race’s popularity has surged, not everyone has been as lucky. Soonchil Shin, 59, has finished 15 Sydney Marathons but missed out on a place in the 2026 race. Viv Kartsounis has finished 16 previous Sydney Marathons. Wolter Peeters “When I first heard about Sydney Marathon becoming a candidate, I was excited actually because a lot of people [would] come to Australia, and it’s good for business, good for the economy,” Shin said. “This year, I missed out even though I uploaded my application for the ballot. But, I wasn’t chosen, I wasn’t taken. It was surprising.”

Blogger Brian Rock analysed the data from those who finished the 2026 race and found that Australians made up 90 per cent of the field in 2023 but just 39 per cent of the total runners this year. Disappointed, Shin was one of several Bridge Club runners who contacted race organisers about missing out. Kartsounis’ collection of medals from racing in the Sydney Marathon. Wolter Peeters “I sent a private message saying ‘you didn’t look after Bridge Club members’,” he said, adding that he mentioned the New York Marathon in his message, which, along with several schemes to lock in places for local runners, has guaranteed entry for those who have done 15 or more previous editions. Organisers told Shin they were looking into it. Then, last month, club members received an email in the days before the general ballot opened to tell them 100 spots had been set aside for its members, meaning all would get a spot in the 2027 race.

title: Before weighing into the immigration debate, spend a night in hospital
text:
Advertisement

NationalImmigration Opinion Before weighing into the immigration debate, spend a night in hospital Brendan Nicholson Writer October 18, 2026 — 1:30pm

October 18, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

It’s time for a serious reality check. Anyone trying to weigh the so-called “immigration debate” should spend some time in an Australian hospital. Anyone who has spent time in an Australian hospital knows that the healthcare system runs on the labour of migrants. Getty Immigration is being used cynically as a political wedge by those harking after a long-gone monoculture without regard for facts or practical consequences. I recently spent several days in hospital where my experience before, during and after an operation demonstrated how deluded and dangerous this low-grade politics is. Any healthcare experience is a reminder that more than half the Australian population was born overseas or has at least one parent born overseas. My blood samples were taken days before by technicians of Nepalese and Indian heritage. The taxi driver who turned up at 5.40am to take me to hospital was a cheerful bloke from Delhi who took me straight to the correct entrance in a sprawl of medical facilities.

Advertisement

Related Article Opinion

Immigration I’m sick of immigration being blamed for problems it doesn’t cause Ross Gittins Economics Editor I was prepared for my operation by a nurse of Nepalese origin. Then I was put under by an alert anaesthetist from India who’d rung me in advance to check on a mistake I’d made in my paperwork. The surgery was carried out by an excellent doctor of Pakistani origin, who explained carefully and clearly before the operation what would be done, and why. Over the next five days I was cared for by nurses whose families were from India, Nepal, the Philippines, Tibet and Ethiopia; a cosmopolitan mix of Muslims, Hindus, Christians and others, along with several we would once have classified as Anglo-Celtics. If the politicians pushing the anti-immigration line could instantly send most of these people “home”, those of us connected to medical devices would have awakened to a largely still and silent building, sadly missing their skills and cheerful approach. The anti-immigration lot will throw up their hands and say that of course they don’t mean to banish “those” immigrants. That’s not the point.

Advertisement

The reality is that with an ageing population and declining birthrate, cynically harking back to the White Australia era risks unleashing racism that can dishearten and discourage people that our workforce badly needs. Loading That lowest common denominator debate and the way it’s being delivered – basically blaming immigrants for everything – is highly offensive, unsophisticated and riddled with misinformation and contradictions. Having a multicultural society brings great benefits and we’ll be in serious trouble if they all go “home”. Certainly, fix any rorts but leave the rest alone. Related Article Opinion

Immigration Why no number of new migrants will ever satisfy Australian-born citizens Parnell Palme McGuinness Columnist and communications adviser

Advertisement

Otherwise, who will fill the huge gaps among highly skilled specialists across many professions, not only in medicine. Who will care for our elderly and those in the NDIS, staff our supermarkets, pick our fruit, build our houses – not to forget providing flair, skill and glamour in our assorted football codes? Just over half the doctors newly registered in Australia in recent years obtained their primary medical qualifications overseas. Well over a third of medical specialists in Australia are internationally trained. At least a third – and probably more – of nurses in Australia were born overseas and about 17 per cent of them obtained their nursing qualifications before coming to Australia. The rest studied nursing in Australia. Well over 40 per cent of Australia’s aged and disability carers and registered nurses were born overseas.

Advertisement

Those in the medical profession who were born abroad are aware of the anti-immigration rhetoric and say it’s not unique to Australia. A willingness to blame migrants for personal or financial difficulties drives such movements in countries including the US, Germany, The Netherlands and Britain. They note that migrants who establish businesses are often very ambitious and entrepreneurial. Many have done so to pursue new ideas, to utilise their skills and experience, to achieve greater financial and professional independence. Others because it took time to have their overseas qualifications recognised, to overcome language barriers, or because they had limited local networks. Some made a strategic decision to establish a business to utilise their cultural knowledge, international experience, professional skills and connections with overseas markets. Over time, these professionals say, self-employment rates among migrants have reached or exceeded those of the broader Australian population and about a third of small businesses in Australia are owned by migrants. Other assumptions made about immigrants are simply wrong, as in the idea that those accepted in Australia as refugees will be a lifelong drain on the rest of us. Related Article Opinion

Immigration nation I am the child of an immigrant. So are 51 per cent of Australians Eryk Bagshaw Investigative reporter

Advertisement

It shouldn’t surprise that some of those brave and enterprising enough to escape horrors in their homelands, also demonstrate significant entrepreneurial skills once they settle in Australia. We benefit enormously from this injection of talent and drive. On the day before my hospital visit, my hair was cut by a man who was born in Iraq and later escaped to Turkey as a refugee. He made it to Australia, runs his own business and speaks Arabic, Turkish and English. A highly skilled immigrant who has prospered in Australia, he observed that there were, of course, some flaws in Australia’s migration system, and the government was working to address them. But, he said, most migrants worked extremely hard and were not dependent on Centrelink payments. “Migrant-owned businesses make an important contribution to Australia’s economy through employment, innovation, investment and economic activity, while also providing migrants with an alternative pathway to professional and financial independence,” he said. Those driving the toxic and superficial immigration debate need to consider the practical realities of our country and the talented and diverse mix of people who make it work.

Advertisement

A big part of this is noticing what our migrant population does for all of us and thinking through what our nation would be like without them. Poorer in every way. title: Northern rivals aren’t the All Blacks: Why bruised Wallabies still have spring tour belief

SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby Northern rivals aren’t the All Blacks: Why bruised Wallabies still have spring tour belief Iain Payten October 18, 2026 — 1:27pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Star flanker Fraser McReight says the Wallabies will embark on the spring tour bruised but still armed with belief, having taken harsh lessons from a one-sided Bledisloe Cup campaign and knowing they won’t face any sides in the UK with the same attacking potency as the All Blacks. Having gone six games undefeated – the latter five under new coach Les Kiss – the Wallabies came down to earth with a giant thud during a brutal eight-day stretch against New Zealand, in which the Kiwis thumped Australia by a combined score of 93-40 in two dominant victories. Loading The All Blacks effectively repelled the Wallabies’ attack, and were a class above with the ball, scoring 14 tries to six during the series with breakdown dominance and skill. Dave Rennie’s side scored six tries in a white-hot opening half at Accor Stadium on Saturday, ending the contest well before half-time. The humbling trans-Tasman series was a massive reality check for the Wallabies ahead of a big spring tour in November, in which they will play England, Scotland, Wales and a yet-to-be determined fourth side in the Nations Championship finals.

Advertisement

But Australian players were attempting to keep a sense of perspective after Saturday’s game, based on the quality of the All Blacks’ performance, to ensure all confidence gained this winter isn’t stripped away. Fraser McReight (white headgear) makes a tackle on Peter Lakai in Sydney on Saturday. AP “If we were saying we’re going to go into the Bledisloe unbeaten, we’re taking that,” McReight said. “We beat some really good teams, had some tough opposition and some tough, close games. But the ABs are world class for a reason. They’re top two in the world and I don’t think there’s many teams that attack like that: very fast and direct and decisive. “It was a great test for us, and we learned a lot last week, albeit the scoreline wasn’t great. Same for today, we’ll learn a lot. You just can’t give a team 22 points – given they’re the top two in the world – can’t give them 22 points head start.” McReight repeated the point about the potency of the world No.2 All Blacks when asked about the Wallabies’ belief heading into the spring tour.

Advertisement

“No other teams in the northern hemisphere that we’re versing – I guess Scotland maybe a little bit, but not at the ABs’ level – attack like that,” he said. Max Jorgensen tries to conjure something for the Wallabies. Getty Images “So for us, we’re versing the best and adapting to the best, so what’s next rung? England’s first up, they love a high high-kick game, they’ve got some big forwards, quick outside backs. “It is tough over there, but we really relish northern hemisphere teams and especially playing in England. In ’24 we had a great win and last year we’re in that match until the kind of 65th minute, and it kind of went away from us. So the belief is there, and we’ve just got to keep working and taking lessons.” “Lessons” are a modern-day go-to for a losing dressing room, but the return of several significant starting players for the spring tour will provide a more tangible boost for the Wallabies. Coach Les Kiss confirmed Carter Gordon (broken leg), Hunter Paisami (suspension), Len Ikitau (concussion) and Ben Donaldson (groin) will all be good to tour, and Tom Hooper and Taniela Tupou will also rejoin the squad after stints with their clubs.

Advertisement

Halfback Ryan Lonergan conceded the confidence of the Wallabies had taken a “pretty big hit”, but said they’d been provided with “a good wake-up call” by the All Blacks about being clinical when given chances to score. The Wallabies had small windows to remain in the fight against the Kiwis, by scoring and building scoreboard pressure, but mostly failed to execute. Max Jorgensen scores the match-winner at Twickenham in 2024. Stan Sport “It’s a great challenge to be able to play the All Blacks twice. Now we know where we’re at,” Lonergan said. “You miss the mark a little bit against the All Blacks, they make you pay with the pace that they play at. We know that even through Super Rugby that if you’re a little bit off, particularly around that collision area, they can make you pay because they’re such good footballers.” Rennie conceded New Zealand had focused on winning the breakdown, to negate the effectiveness of McReight, who he rated as “the best in the world” at poaching and disrupting a team’s recycle speed.

Advertisement

Having either been targeted by runners to make a tackle (he made a team high 19 in Sydney and 16 in Auckland) or with arriving players cleaning him out, McReight failed to win a single turnover in Sydney, and two successes in Auckland amounted to nought given the All Blacks had the penalty advantage. “I didn’t really get too many clean opportunities to be fair. I tried to make a mess of it a lot of times,” McReight said. Of the many lessons learnt, Lonergan said an important one was being more clinical when on attack in the opponent’s quarter. Several try-scoring opportunities were either lost through poor skill execution, passing choices or just the ability to keep dominating contact. Related Article Exclusive

Australian rugby ‘We didn’t share the same values’: Rennie breaks long silence on his Wallabies axing “Previously this year, we’ve stayed quite patient and we’ve been really, really good down there in that zone,” Lonergan said. “The last couple of weeks, we’re just missing that execution a little bit. It’s as simple as a pass sometimes. Our structures down there in that zone haven’t changed much – credit to their defence. They’ve really sent the two into that contact and slowed our ball down.”

An international mining giant has taken its $38 billion pursuit of Australia’s largest gold producer directly to local investors, offering them the muscle to build a globally competitive gold behemoth and hoping their pressure will help force the board to the negotiating table. Executives from South African-based miner Gold Fields brought forward plans for an Australian investor roadshow last week, seeking to boost its profile and win over key fund managers after Western Australia’s Northern Star Resources rejected its takeover attempt as “highly opportunistic”. Gold Fields chief executive Mike Fraser has been meeting with Northern Star’s institutional investors across Perth, Sydney and Melbourne. Ross Swanborough Gold Fields chief executive Mike Fraser spent the week meeting with Northern Star’s institutional investors across Perth, Sydney and Melbourne, noting that there appeared to be widespread consensus on the “strategic logic” of the tie-up. Slides shown at investor briefings stated that combining the two companies’ projects in Western Australia would forge a new global gold production powerhouse in a “world-class province”, capable of rivalling Barrick and Newmont Corporation’s Nevada Gold Mines joint venture in the United States, and Agnico Eagle’s Abitibi hub in Canada.

Advertisement

If the takeover ultimately succeeds, the combined group would rank as the second-biggest gold producer globally, behind Denver-based Newmont. It would control eight of Australia’s 20 biggest gold mines – including Northern Star’s massive “Super Pit” in Kalgoorlie – and produce 4.1 million ounces a year of the precious metal. Northern Star’s Kalgoorlie Super Pit is one of Australia’s largest open-cut gold mines. Trevor Collens “Creating a truly competitive global mining gold major that is centred out of WA is something that’s quite compelling in our view,” Fraser said. In an interview in Melbourne, Fraser revealed that his discussions with Northern Star began more than a year ago after, Gold Fields acquired a 3.5 per cent stake in the company via its acquisition of Gold Road. While some investors are pressing Gold Fields to sweeten its bid after Northern Star rejected its initial shares-and-cash proposal for being too low, Fraser is urging the board to first hold talks with Gold Fields, agree to the merits of the tie-up and grant access to its books.

Advertisement

Related Article Updated

Gold Australia’s biggest gold miner rejects ‘opportunistic’ $38b takeover offer “Let’s agree [to] the strategic logic of it and align that this is something we want to pursue,” he said. “I think if we can then go in and do due diligence, firm up the value, then we can have a conversation around value.” However, Northern Star chairman Michael Chaney said the board maintained that Gold Fields’ proposal did not appropriately recognise the quality and long-term value of the company’s portfolio of high-quality, long-life gold assets in tier-one mining jurisdictions, and its growth profile. He said the company’s directors remained focused on acting in shareholders’ best interests. “This includes engaging with parties on proposals that represent value above what we believe Northern Star can generate as a standalone company,” Chaney said. “The Gold Fields proposal was not in that category.” Under Gold Fields’ initial offer, Northern Star shareholders would have received 0.3125 new Gold Fields shares and $7.25 in cash for each share they own. The bid valued Northern Star at $38.7 billion, a 22 per cent premium based on both companies’ share prices on the last trading date before it was lobbed.

Advertisement

Editor's pick Gold Getting married? There’s a new chart to check before buying a ring Northern Star’s shares are now more than 10 per cent higher than they were the day before news of the Gold Fields approach leaked. “At current market values, the Gold Fields proposal is now at a discount to Northern Star’s share price,” Chaney said. One of the top shareholders whose support Gold Fields is seeking to rally is US-based activist investor Elliott Investment Management, which has built a 6 per cent stake in Northern Star and has been pressuring the board to make sweeping changes. The hedge fund has criticised Northern Star’s sharemarket underperformance this year and urged it to consider a sale or asset divestments. Gold Fields’ attempted takeover of Northern Star follows a multi-year rally in gold prices, fuelled by intensifying geopolitical tensions, worsening inflation fears, erratic policymaking in the United States and an erosion of trust in the US dollar.

Advertisement

Gold, the precious metal prized by civilisations for thousands of years for its rarity and use in jewellery, tends to be most sought after these days by investors as a safe place to store wealth during periods of extreme financial uncertainty. Investors said the approach for Northern Star reflected the growing strategic appeal of gold miners. “Gold miners are back in favour,” Betashares investment strategist Tom Wickenden said. Na Djinang Circus | Ocker

Civic Hall Ballarat, until October 25 Five performers from First Nations-led company Na Djinang Circus navigate the crowd while delivering death-defying circus stunts in the middle of Fed Square. We turn back in time to a pre-colonial era as dramatic, otherworldly music plays in the background. The troupe roves through the crowd as if hunting, then gathers on a platform. The intimate audience of onlookers grows once the public realise that something is afoot. Na Djinang Circus show Ocker. Tiffany Garvie The choreography is dynamic, as the artists impressively run and tumble through people and across the stairs, doing lifts and climbing on one another. Embedding Indigenous knowledge in contemporary movements, performers emulate animals and cultural practices. They cleverly introduce props – a ladder and a trolley – carrying and manoeuvring them across the flat and cobbled surfaces of the square. They mount the ladder, balancing on its rungs like a tightrope or handstand-style, then lay it on the ground like train tracks to ride the trolley over it, as if it’s a raft sailing along the Yarra River. Surprising and ever-moving, this place-based show is an exhilarating watch.

Darby James | Little Squirt

Ballarat Mechanics’ Institute, until October 24 Darby James in Little Squirt. Liv Morison In the depths of Melbourne’s lockdowns in 2021, Darby James clicked on a Facebook ad for sperm donation. The UK-born musical comedian premiered his one-man cabaret based on the experience at Melbourne Fringe 2023 as Spunk Daddy, and this week performed its 100th show at the same festival. Little Squirt is distinctly contemporary, wrestling with some of modern life’s heaviest dilemmas. Dressed as a seaman (say it out loud), James ponders the ethics of having biological children as a cis gay man, and what it means to have a legacy. The performer is a master of tone, somehow striking a perfect balance between ejaculation jokes and moving monologues, all with his tightly controlled vocals. The audience responds in kind, from raucous laughter to stunned silence. Tech issues on opening night mean that James is unplugged, adding an extra layer of intimacy to this already deeply intimate and thoughtful show.

title: Sam Pang is the most popular man on TV. Now what?
text:
